items.en: Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.

Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.
According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.

That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.

In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”

To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark, which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks. According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.

“We put a tremendous amount of effort into making sure your model can remember what’s important to you over days, weeks, months, and beyond,” said research scientist Kavya Kopparapu in a video accompanying the launch.

The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year. Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.
According to the post, the models were trained at Meta’s Prometheus data center in central Ohio, which came online earlier this year.
Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.

A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Brimstone and its one-stop process for making cleaner cement and critical minerals
Brimstone is a code-switching climate tech company for these polarized political times. The US startup is part green cement company, part critical mineral producer.

During the Biden administration, its primary pitch was cement that generates about 60% fewer greenhouse-gas emissions. It achieves this by switching to silicate rocks instead of standard limestone, which releases carbon dioxide when heated.
Under the Trump administration, however, the company is emphasizing another benefit of its process: the ability to extract valuable materials from those same rocks.
Job titles of the future: Delivery drone air traffic controller

The moment Trevor Wischnewsky heard that drones were delivering pizza and sushi around his Texas neighborhood, his mind was made up. “It was super fascinating,” he says. “I just immediately wanted to be a part of it.”

Wischnewsky is now an RPIC, or remote pilot in command, at a company called FlyTrex. An RPIC is like an air traffic controller. But instead of airplanes, they oversee fleets of drones that ferry cargo to homes and businesses

Geoffrey Hinton tells us why he’s now scared of the tech he helped build

Geoffrey Hinton is a pioneer of deep learning who helped develop some of the most important techniques at the heart of modern artificial intelligence, but after a decade at Google, he’s stepped down to focus on concerns he now has about AI.

Hinton is now spending his time on what he describes as “more philosophical work.” And that will focus on the small but—to him—very real danger that AI will turn out to be a disaster. Here’s why he’s so worried.

Obsession, the horror film everyone is still talking about, centers on a deceptively simple warning: Be careful what you wish for. A hopeless romantic, desperate for his crush’s love and attention, wanders into a magic shop, where a red-and-yellow box catches his eye amid a display of otherwise banal knickknacks. Inside is the One Wish Willow, a magic stick that promises to grant its owner a single wish within 24 hours. With its bright colors and old-timey comic-book design, it looks as harmless as a prize pulled from a Cracker Jack box. Instead of giving this cute novelty gift to his beloved, he uses it himself, wishing she would love him more than anything else in the world. From there, a universe of terror unfolds.

Obsession’s popularity foretold that magic, mysticism, and spirituality would continue to have a moment in the wider culture. This summer, the Morgan Library & Museum opened “Tarot! Renaissance Symbols, Modern Visions,” an exhibition exploring tarot’s artistic influence on expressions of spirituality and identity. Vogue recently published a story about designer Gabriela Hearst’s daily tarot practice, placing her in a tradition that includes Christian Dior and Maria Grazia Chiuri, both of whom have turned to the cards for divine guidance and creative inspiration. Burberry’s spring 2027 ready-to-wear collection features two trench coats printed with tarot cards, while actress Lucy Hale revealed during a recent Architectural Digest house tour that she, too, pulls a card every day.

The interest in the occult extends far beyond tarot. In October, the Palm Springs Art Museum will close “A Queer Arcana: Art, Magic, and Spirit,” an exhibition exploring the influence of magic, spirituality, and esoteric knowledge on queer art and culture. Last year, Florence + the Machine released Everybody Scream, an album inspired by witchcraft and mysticism. The Toledo Museum of Art recently closed “Cursed! The Power of Magic in the Ancient World,” which examined the role of magic in ancient societies. I have friends who, three years ago, didn’t even know their sun sign but now speak fluently about the hell that was their Saturn return. These moments are possible because more people feel empowered to speak openly about their spiritual practices; every year, the subject becomes a little less taboo.

Personally, spirituality has always been a door I’ve liked to walk through — an openness passed down to me by my mother. Growing up, she was obsessed with angels, a preoccupation that verged on hoarding anything with wings. Instead of books or family photographs, angel figurines lined our shelves. They were her prized possessions, a type of lifeline. In actuality, they were a shrine in honor of the angels who saved her life the night she attempted suicide.

The last time I heard her tell the story, I was probably 10 years old, so some of the details have blurred. But at some point in her life, my mother tried to kill herself. On the brink of death, she was visited by angels, who brought her to her brother and father. In this vision, they greeted her with warmth and love, told her it wasn’t her time, and sent her back to Earth. Whatever my mother believed before that experience, afterward she was devout. Having felt the other side once, she became engrossed in connecting with it however she could. I have vivid memories of falling asleep on her friends’ couches while they smoked cigarettes and read tarot cards. I didn’t really understand what the cards did. To me, they were magic tokens that predicted the future. I would sit quietly on the couch, watching each card flip with anticipation. The Nine of Swords made me feel sad and anxious. The Magician felt powerful. The Hanged Man always scared me. But opening myself to that connection never did.

As I’ve moved cities, ended relationships, and ached to connect with my mother after her passing 15 years ago, my curiosity about the spiritual has only grown, particularly my impulse to turn to it for answers to life’s most impossible questions. I have a restless but exacting nature. My Gemini sun can see a dozen possibilities, while my Virgo rising feels compelled to analyze every one of them. With both placements ruled by Mercury, the planet of communication, I’m constantly searching for more information, more context — anything that might help me avoid making the wrong decision and having to live with regret.

That hunger for certainty has led me to try a little bit of everything: I consider astrology to be an incredible tool for understanding myself. I’m also an avid tarot user and make an effort to pull cards every few days for updates on whatever lessons the universe is attempting to teach me. I’ve hired many an Etsy witch (embarrassingly, based on recommendations from TikTok), from whom I have purchased glamour spells to make me more alluring and compelling, money spells to improve my finances, and cleansing spells to rid me of bad energy. I’ve also paid for spells intended to make an ex come back, regret their wrongdoings, or think about me nonstop. If the One Wish Willow were real, I would probably be dealing with the repercussions right now.

My own experience with magical blowback has been far less cinematic. There’s a little witch shop in East Hollywood — the shelves lined with old, sticky bottles and glass jars filled with herbs — where you can buy ingredients to make your own potions or ask the practitioner to mix one for you. I once attempted a spell myself using candles, oils, and rose petals and wound up leaving a huge burn mark on my vintage dining table. Not everything works. Not everything is certain. And yet some of my experiences have been shockingly accurate.

My first uncanny encounter with a spirit medium was with Jessica Lanyadoo. I met Jessica by happenstance while perusing the booths at San Francisco’s West Coast Craft in 2017, where she was offering 15-minute tarot readings. Inside an intimate booth behind a pink curtain, Jessica picked up on my energy and began a traditional session. About halfway through, however, she stopped to tell me that in addition to reading tarot, she was a medium and she believed my mother was there.

Jessica sat quietly, her eyes drifting away from me and her head cocked slightly, as though someone were whispering in her ear. She seemed taken aback. Then she looked at me intensely, flattening her palm against her heart, and with a slight tap, she said, “Wow, your mom really loves you so much.” I almost burst into tears.

My mother was a woman who felt things very deeply — a quality, for better or worse, she passed along to me. Our feelings can become almost unbearable, taking on a physical weight in our bodies. Whenever my mother was overwhelmed by an emotion, often sadness or love, she would flatten her palm against her heart and tap it, as though that single gesture might steady its beating. I had never seen anyone else do it. I just knew Jessica could see her. That was all I needed: I booked a full session with her the next day. Her waiting list was six months long.

Half a year later, I found myself in Jessica’s little back house in Oakland, and I still remember the intensity of crossing its threshold. The air itself felt different there, the way I imagine it must have felt for the children in A Wrinkle in Time to travel from one dimension to another. Heavy but limitless. I wish I could say I spent the bulk of this time asking about my mother or my career, which we did discuss with eerily accurate insight from Jessica … but at the end of the day, what I really wanted to talk about was love.

At the top of my list was one of the most intense relationships of my life: an affair with a professor who taught at my university. He was tall and somewhat handsome, but I became intrigued after learning that he wrote for one of my favorite websites. He was never actually my professor, so there were no winks in the middle of class or extra credit for “extracurriculars.” In hindsight, I think I pursued him just for the plot. I had seen professor-student relationships in movies so many times that I felt as though I was doing college wrong if I didn’t sleep with a professor when I had the chance. It was all a cliché, and yet I fell naïvely, ridiculously in love and longed for him years after I should have let go. Here was my chance to get the certainty I needed. And Jessica did not sugarcoat.

“This man is a liar!” She said bluntly. “I have a name for men like this: a bathtub man. He’s the kind of man that can only have good sex and good boners if there’s love involved.” She explained that he was the kind of person who would know when you had a hard day and tell you to sit down while he runs you a bath and lights candles. Then, the next thing you know, your bathtub is flooded and he’s nowhere to be found. “He just wants to ruin your life because it gives him the greatest feeling about who he is — and also a really good boner.” She told me that when I was in my early 30s, I would want to murder him. And now in my early 30s, hypothetically speaking, she’s totally right. He would ruin my life more than once, popping in and out for years, until our last meeting, which resulted in a huge blowout screaming match in some Middle America hotel, where he packed his bags and left after drinking half a bottle of my very expensive wine.

After an assessment like that, I had to ask what she thought about my then-boyfriend. She asked me to say his name aloud, and when I did, a smile spread across her face. “I really like him.” She told me he was a lovely, caring person who was deeply in love with me. “The parts of yourself that you really think are not okay, he likes.” That struck me hard. At the time, I constantly questioned whether I was a good person and punished myself whenever I fell short. But he saw how hard I tried and adored me, faults and all. She told me he would teach me how to love and be loved and he would remain an important person in my life for a very long time. “You have a sweet life with him.”

Then she stopped. She put her head down for a brief moment, her brown curls bouncing over the top of her bright-red glasses. “I don’t think you’re going to marry him,” she said before moving on, like someone who slams a door without realizing how loud the bang will be. After eight years together, he proposed to me in a rowboat on Lake Bled in Slovenia. I remember thinking, Jessica was wrong! Until 11 months later, when we sat at our kitchen table in L.A. and decided to end our relationship. She had been right. Looking back, she had also been right about the sweetness too. Though he wasn’t the one, we’d had a very sweet life together.

Jessica no longer does personal readings, but the next reader to come close to that accuracy was a woman named Sonia who conducts readings over the phone from her home in England. Sonia asks a seemingly random mix of questions that rarely make sense in the moment but that I now understand are clues about what’s coming. During our first conversation, she asked, “Are you studying anything at the moment?” I told her not really, aside from some French lessons I was taking online. Throughout the reading, she also asked whether I recognized two men’s names. I didn’t. Then she told me I would meet a tall man in January with brown hair and intense eyes, someone I would really like. It might be long-distance, she said. She warned me to be careful: He would tell me he wanted a relationship, but when things became serious, he would probably disappear.
Three weeks later, I matched with a French man on Hinge after he wrote to me, “I can’t believe we’re still strangers.”

He was tall with dark, slightly curly hair and large deep-brown eyes. The two names Sonia had mentioned turned out to form his Instagram handle. His profile said he was in L.A., and it wasn’t until we had been chatting for five days that I realized he was only visiting. He actually lived in France. True to my tendency to do things for the story, I embarked on a whirlwind romance with him, spending nearly every night of his trip together. Before he left, he gave me a beautiful flower ring to remember him by. But we never stopped talking. We spoke every day, from sunup in L.A. until sunset in Paris, and I fell more deeply in love with him than I had with anyone before. Months later, I flew across the world to visit him, and after walking the streets of Paris, he surprised me with a stay at a seaside château in Marseille, where I met his best friends. And then, about a week after I returned home, he abruptly ended things, telling me he wasn’t ready to be in a relationship again. It has been gutting. But it unfolded almost exactly as Sonia said it would.

Then again, believing in the mystical does not mean believing every mystic. Just a few weeks ago, I tried a new reader on the Westside of L.A. who, after already charging $80 for the reading, tried to persuade me to spend an additional $750 on a love spell to get the French man back, saying that “it would be the only way to clear his blockages.” I politely and quickly, declined. My favorite TikTok tarot reader used to say, “Take what rings true and leave what doesn’t.” And I find that to be valuable advice.

Ultimately, a reading is never a verdict. At its best, it can give you language for truths you already feel in your gut but haven’t been able to articulate. Sonia always reminds me that you have to leave room for movement: energy shifts, circumstances change, and something that feels true one day may not be true the next. That’s just life. And in my insatiable conquest to find all the answers, I often have found myself with more questions. I still haven’t met the one. I still question my choices daily. And I still ache for my mother, her arms around me, and to know what she might say to help as I struggle to get through the days. The anxiety is excruciating, and I’m reminded of the way she’d soothe her own heart with the drumming of her palm.
Maybe it’s the human condition to want the answers when the only real answer is that there are none. Then again, I’d rather ask the cards.

For Larry David, the 1980s began with so much promise. After years of rejection — from women, from employers, from audiences seeking laughter — it seemed that Larry’s luck had finally changed. Following a nationwide talent search, he had been selected as one of nine young comics to star on ABC’s new late-night sketch show, Fridays. This was it, the proverbial big break. And one with such promise that Larry was even willing to leave his native New York for L.A.

Well … as it turned out, Larry’s big break didn’t quite go according to plan. And four years later, he was back in New York with less confidence than when he had left. Nevertheless, he soon managed to secure another great late-night opportunity — this time as a writer for the tenth season of Saturday Night Live.

Admittedly, SNL circa 1984 was not quite the juggernaut it had once been. And yeah, sure, this would be one of those weird-in-retrospect seasons where the show existed without Lorne Michaels. But still, from a certain angle and in a certain light, Larry could squint his way into seeing this new gig at SNL as a second chance at something.

Though, of course, because Larry is Larry (and therefore governed by a peculiar physics that dictates that every step forward be followed by two in reverse), his year at SNL would prove to be far from a rosy adventure.
Excerpt from 'Emperor of Nothing: The Making of Larry David'
“I don’t remember a lot about my time at SNL,” Larry admits, “but I do remember something that happened early on. Like during my second or third week. And it must have been a Tuesday night.”

Tuesday nights were crunch time at SNL because Wednesday afternoons were when writers would present their sketches for read-through. But for Larry, who routinely finished his sketches quickly, there was no need for a crunch.

“Well,” Larry explains, “at least that’s what I thought. But there I am: It’s Tuesday night, maybe seven o’clock, and I have two or three sketches ready for read-through [tomorrow], so I walk to the elevator and push the button. I’m ready to go home. But then the elevator arrives and one of the people who gets out is Dick [Ebersol].”
Being a cordial person, Larry wished his new boss a pleasant evening. But instead of reciprocating, Ebersol looked suddenly annoyed.
“What are you doing?” Ebersol asked. “Where are you going?”
“Oh, I’m going home,” Larry answered, which clearly wasn’t the right answer.
“He looked at me like I was crazy!” Larry recalls. “He said, ‘What do you mean you’re “going home”?’”
“Well,” Larry explained to Ebersol, “I’ve written three sketches and a couple of news pieces. So, you know, I’m good to go. That’s it.”
Ebersol shook his head. No, that was not it.
“On Tuesdays,” Ebersol explained, “we stay up all night.”
“Because that’s when we write the show.”
“But I’ve already written three pieces.”
To Ebersol, this didn’t matter. Larry could have written a million pieces.
“On Tuesdays,” Ebersol repeated firmly, “we stay here all night.”
Larry knew he had a decision to make: Go home and get a good night’s sleep, or stick around and … do what? Just walk around the office and pretend to look busy?

“What did it matter whether I was there or not?” Larry says, laughing at the memory of this unexpected standoff. “So I wished him good luck and I got in the elevator. That seemed like the right decision. Though, looking back, I think that was the beginning of the end for me.”
It was. And from there, things quickly got worse.
BY OCTOBER 1984, Larry was officially fed up. The season’s fifth episode, hosted by George Carlin, was just about to go live, and once again — at the last minute — Larry’s sketch had been cut.

“So I go up to Dick Ebersol,” Larry recalls. “He’s in his chair. He’s got the headphones on. It’s maybe five minutes before the show is gonna start. And there I am, with smoke coming out of my nose, and I’m just hell-bent on telling him off.”
There must have been 40 or 50 people racing around, frantically getting ready for the show. “Hey, Dick,” Larry said.
Slowly, and only half paying attention, Dick Ebersol turned to Larry. “Yeah?”
“THIS FUCKING SHOW STINKS!” Larry shouted. “IT’S AWFUL! IT’S TERRIBLE! AND IT’S GETTING WORSE EVERY WEEK. YOU SHOULD BE EMBARRASSED. I’M EMBARRASSED. I’M DONE. I’VE HAD IT. I QUIT!!”

Ebersol was so taken aback by this outburst that he was rendered momentarily speechless. But that didn’t matter. Because just as quickly as Larry got the words out, he stormed out of the building. And then triumphantly, as a now-free man, he walked through the streets back to his apartment.

“Well, that [triumphant feeling] quickly wore off,” Larry explains. “It didn’t take very long. Maybe only a few blocks. And now, as I’m walking home, I start to compute how much money I just cost myself.”
By his estimation, the money that he’d just sacrificed would have probably been enough to get him through the next 18 months.
“I’m an idiot,” Larry explained to Kenny Kramer after arriving back at his apartment in Manhattan Plaza. “What the hell am I gonna do?”
Clearly, Larry had intended this to be a question about the broader future. As in, How the hell am I going to get another job? Who’s gonna hire me after this?
Kramer, however, considered the question in a different way — thinking instead of an unconventional solution that might allow Larry to undo what he’d just done.
“Maybe you can just go back?” Kramer suggested. “Go back?” Larry repeated, dumbstruck.
“Yeah,” Kramer said. “Pretend like it never happened.”
“You mean … just walk into the staff meeting Monday morning like it never happened?”
“Sure! You’re an emotional person. People don’t take you seriously!”
“So I just … go back? And pretend the whole thing never happened?”
It wasn’t like Larry had any better ideas. So, the following Monday morning, Larry showed up for work at Saturday Night Live.

“I take my seat at the morning meeting,” Larry remembers. “And, of course, all the writers are staring at me. They’re looking at me like, ‘Are you crazy? Didn’t you quit? What the hell are you doing here?’ But no one actually says anything and so I’m just sitting there, trying my best to act like nothing’s happened. Meanwhile, Dick is going around the room and asking each writer what they’ve got planned for the week. Then finally, he gets to me.”
“Larry?” Ebersol asked. “Yes,” Larry replied.
This was it — the moment of truth! And after a tense second or two, it swung in Larry’s favor.
“He didn’t say a thing about me quitting,” Larry explains.
Instead, Ebersol just wanted to know if Larry had any ideas for the next show. And he did.
“I’ve got this idea about a circus family,” Larry began. “You know, one of those families of performers, like the Flying Wallendas …”

Larry went on, continuing to pitch the idea. Though by the time he drilled down into the details, it was already clear: Larry’s own little circus routine had been a success. The scheme had worked, Kenny Kramer was a savant, and somehow, miraculously, Larry had managed to un-quit his job.

AS LARRY REACCLIMATED TO LIFE IN NEW YORK, he began to furnish his sparse apartment. This process included buying a physics-defying piece of furniture that without aid of magic could toggle between both a bed and sofa — something called a futon. But unfortunately, after the whole rigmarole of buying it, having it delivered, and setting it up in his apartment, Larry decided to return the futon.

So the vendor, Arise Futon, sent over one of their deliverymen: a 20-something kid who during his off hours had been moonlighting as a stand-up. Since this kid — who performed under the name Jackie Roberts — was just at the start of his comedy career, there was no reason why Larry would have known him. But the kid knew exactly who Larry was. So, he gathered up the courage to say something.
“I told him I liked the show Fridays,” the deliveryman recalls, “and asked him why they canceled it.”
“I have hardly any recollection of that,” Larry says about his brief, long-ago interchange with the delivery guy. And why would he? “He was just a guy delivering futons!”

But what was a forgettable moment for Larry was a memorable one for the futon delivery guy — who, shortly after this encounter, would quit the futon game and fully pursue comedy under his given name, Ray Romano.

“Can you believe that guy was Ray?” Larry remarks, amazed all these years later by this odd before-they-were-stars encounter. “So yeah, it’s true; Ray Romano picked up a futon from my apartment. And yeah, he asked me something about why Fridays went off the air.”
Unsurprisingly, Larry has no memory of what he said to his futon deliveryman four decades earlier. But for Ray, the moment was memorable. Especially because what Larry said felt prescient.
“He said,” Ray recalls, “‘Well, that’s television!’ Or something like that.”

SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE IS one of those shows whose staff is constantly turning over. As such, it’s a place where bright-eyed newly hired writers and performers are welcomed with famous stories of yesteryear — including the legendary tale about how Larry David quit and then un-quit SNL.

As legends go, it’s an incredible story. But, really, it’s only half the story. And the other half — the untold half — is almost as amazing. And conveniently, it begins exactly where the other ends: with Larry safely back at work on Monday, pitching an idea about a “circus family.”

“You know, one of those families of performers,” Larry pitched to Ebersol and the other writers in the room, “like the Flying Wallendas …” For those unfamiliar with the Flying Wallendas, Larry explained that they were a family of acrobats who emigrated from Europe and became popular in the 1940s for performing a death-defying high-wire act without the safety of a net below them.

“And they really were a family,” Larry explained, which was relevant not only because it might help explain why these daredevils were so willing to put so much trust in one another, but also because that family dynamic had led him to wonder what it would be like if an outsider tried to gain membership into this sort of high-flying organization.

“The idea,” Larry recalls, “centered around this family of performers who I ended up calling the Flying Zambonis. And, you know, their job is really difficult, but they’ve trained their whole lives to do it. And they’re great! But then one day, they get called in to have a meeting with the circus manager.”

Given their line of work, one might expect that the circus manager — a man named Mr. Drexler — would have deep respect for the family’s aerial artistry. But as it turns out, the aforementioned Drexler is a cigar-chomping maybe-mobster who has an angle of his own.
Listen, I have a little proposition I’d like to make here. How would you like to add another member to the act?
Another member? Are you not satisfied with our work?

No, it’s not that, you’re doing a terrific job. It’s … well, it’s my sister, you see. She’s having a lot of problems with her kid. You know, he’s been out of college a couple years now, and he really doesn’t know what he wants to do. Now, all of a sudden, he’s got this crazy idea in his head that he wants to be a Flying Zamboni. And she came to me and asked if there was anything I can do. And how could I refuse her?
Naturally, the Flying Zambonis are skeptical of adding an unqualified new member.
But, Mr. Drexler, has the boy ever been on the trapeze before?
Then with all due respect, how can he be in the act?
Well, you know, I just thought he’d stand up there on the platform with you. You know, toss the bar out once in a while. You know the way you spin it around …
Sensing the family’s obvious concerns, Mr. Drexler attempts to assuage them by summoning his nephew.

“And that’s when you would come out,” Larry explained to SNL writer Andy Breckman, whom Larry was pitching to play the nephew. “Why me?” Breckman asked. This was certainly a valid question, as SNL had an entire cast of performers, so it was unusual for a writer to be trying to cast another writer. But what made Andy perfect in Larry’s mind was that he didn’t have the same … uh … camera-friendly physique as the show’s actual performers.
“Ohhhhh …” Breckman said, realizing why Larry wanted him. “Because I’m fat.”

“And I wasn’t just overweight,” Breckman says of himself at the time. “I was in my 30s, and I was already balding. I just looked like the epitome of ‘out of shape.’ Which was great for the premise, since the joke was that I’d end up killing the whole family. But, yeah, to answer your question, he wanted to cast me because I was overweight.”

Larry, however, claimed that Breckman’s weight was not the motivation for his casting. At which point Breckman gestured at Larry’s script, where it distinctly noted that the character should be “paunchy” and “ill-equipped” to join the high-wire routine.

Larry explained that he had written the description before even thinking of Breckman. This was purely coincidence! However, Breckman pointed to the dialogue that followed. “But you named the character Andy.”
For a moment, and with minimal sincerity, Larry espoused the many differences between being “fat” and being “paunchy.” But Breckman cut him off.
“Larry,” Breckman said. “I get it. And I think the sketch is hilarious. I’d be honored to do it.”
With Breckman onboard, Larry eventually submitted the final sketch to Ebersol, who thought it was very funny and selected it to be part of that week’s read-through.

“I wish I could tell you how that specific read-through went,” Larry says. “But, really, all those read-throughs blur together into a single memory. And that memory is people laughed a lot, but then the sketch would get cut.”

“This time was different, though,” Breckman points out. “After read-through, Dick Ebersol and his production team were inclined to do it. At least in dress rehearsal. It had made the ‘first cut.’ But they had one stipulation: They, Dick Ebersol and the producers, didn’t want me — just a writer — in the sketch.”

“Look,” Ebersol told Larry in front of the entire cast, as the conversation shifted to his office. “We have ten actual cast members — trained professional actors — who all want airtime and who would all be better on-air. Let’s just figure this out.”

From Larry’s perspective, though, there was nothing to figure out. He conceded that Breckman may have been less “qualified” than the others, but, as Larry made clear, so-called qualifications were irrelevant in this situation. The only thing that really mattered was what would get the most laughs.

“This is where Larry David’s obstinacy comes into play,” Breckman explains. “Or maybe a better word for it is ‘purity.’ Because even back then — back when Larry was struggling to get anything on-air — he was absolutely uncompromising. He kept insisting that ‘no one else’ could do the nephew like me.”
“It needs to be Andy!” Larry told Ebersol. “No, it doesn’t!” Ebersol shot back.

“In retrospect,” Larry says, looking back on this incident, “it probably would have also been funny with someone else in the part. But why wouldn’t you want the sketch to be the funniest it could be?”

“They kept going back and forth,” Breckman recalls. “Larry kept arguing that ‘no one else’ was as out of shape as me. I was, on the one hand, very flattered; on the other hand, kind of insulted! I didn’t know what to say. So I just shut up. I remember just cowering under the table because … it just was insane. It was surreal. These two professionals in a room full of professionals were arguing back and forth about how comically out of shape I was!”
While most of their colleagues looked on in horror, there was one who thought it was hilarious: Julia Louis-Dreyfus, who always enjoyed watching bouts of Larry vs. Ebersol.
“[Those types of situations] were one of the reasons I liked Larry so much,” Julia recalls. “Because he lost his temper.”

Typically, when embroiled in these sorts of escalating back-and-forths, Larry’s go-to move was the quit-and-storm-off. And at some point in his shouting match with Dick Ebersol, the thought of dramatically quitting inevitably did cross Larry’s mind. But there was a problem, of course: He had already done that (and regretted it) less than one week earlier.
“All right,” Larry finally said to Ebersol. “Then let’s not do it.”

Looking back, Breckman says, “It didn’t occur to me until years later, but during his argument with Dick Ebersol, Larry was essentially acting like the manager in his sketch. Granted, Larry’s motivations were pure, but it was still basically the same thing: one guy trying to strong-arm another guy into accepting a substandard performer in their act.”

In Larry’s sketch, the strong-arming proves successful, and Mr. Drexler’s nephew gets to join the Flying Zambonis after all. In real life, however, Larry failed — and, in doing so, became the first SNL writer to ever be the one to cut their own sketch from the show.
MEANWHILE, as both a diligent neighbor and a man of great curiosity, Kenny Kramer made it a point to continue monitoring the top of Larry’s head for potential hair growth.
“Let’s go to the video!” Kramer would reply.
And they did. Every time. Until it became clear to both men that despite all the hope (and all the money the cream had cost), there was no dodging the truth: Larry David was doomed to remain bald.
FOLLICALLY SPEAKING, Larry was a man without prospects. And occupationally — come the end of SNL’s tenth season — Larry found himself without a job and with limited prospects on that end too.

“I don’t remember if they ended up firing me,” Larry says, “or if [it was] because Lorne was coming back to run the show [in place of the Ebersol regime], but it just became clear that I wasn’t going to be returning. Either way, I can’t say I was heartbroken.”
Although Larry’s time at SNL was mostly marked by contention and frustration, he was grateful he had crossed paths with Julia, who left the show the same year and, arguably, was equally disgruntled.

“Larry was just miserable there,” Julia recalls. “[And] it wasn’t a particularly happy experience for me. To begin with, I will take responsibility for some of it, because I was extremely young. I hadn’t graduated college and I was very naïve about how things work in real show business. So I went into it very green … [but] I thought it was going to be a congenial experience; my head was in the clouds. I wasn’t aware of the politicking one had to do, and … Everybody would stay up late. All the work was done between 11 o’clock at night and six o’clock in the morning; that’s when everybody was functioning. And that wasn’t, in my view, conducive to comedy.”
“I don’t really remember any specific conversations [with Julia],” Larry says. “But whenever we did talk, we would always complain about the show.”

Despite Larry’s many frustrations, he did end up managing to get one sketch — a piece called “The Elevator Stool” — on the air. And in an ironic twist, it served as a kind of metaphor for his relationship with Ebersol.

“The sketch,” Larry explains, “was about an architect [played by that week’s host, Ed Begley Jr.,] and he’s pitching a developer [played by Harry Shearer] his plans for a new building. So, you know, it starts with them gathered around, looking at the blueprint.”
At first glance, Harry loves Ed’s plans for this new building, confirming it’s “exactly what I wanted.” But then, just as it seems like a deal will be signed, Harry notices something.
“He’s looking at the blueprint,” Larry continues, “and Harry Shearer says, ‘What’s this?’ And Ed Begley Jr. says, ‘Oh, that’s a stool for the elevator man.’”
Well, if it’s all the same to you, I’d prefer you take it out.
Well, it seems obvious: I don’t want my elevator man sitting on a stool.
Instead of accepting the developer’s request, however, the architect pushes back.
Wait just a second. I’m not saying that they should be sitting in the elevator when they’re taking people up and down. But when they’re waiting in the lobby, I think they should be able to sit.

From there, things continue to escalate. No matter how many seemingly reasonable points Ed Begley Jr. makes (e.g., “Is it wrong to believe that people should have a place to sit?”), Harry Shearer isn’t having it. The stool must go!
“The whole thing just deteriorates into a fight about whether or not the elevator man should be allowed to sit when there are no passengers in the elevator,” Larry explains.
And in the end — like Dick Ebersol — Harry Shearer is only willing to accept a subordinate’s vision if it’s executed to his exact specifications.
And in the end — like Larry David — Ed Begley Jr. simply, stubbornly, and eventually quite angrily refuses to give in.

Pamela Jackson was seven months pregnant when she began to experience radiating, debilitating back pain. At first, she thought she might be in labor, but a stress test at the hospital proved the baby was fine. While Jackson was there, she vomited bile so was sent for a CT scan and an MRI without contrast. Both suggested she had pancreatitis, or inflammation of the pancreas. After a few days in the hospital, she was discharged. Her pain persisted for the next two months, up until the delivery of her daughter, five days before her due date. Soon after the birth, Jackson underwent another MRI, this time with contrast, and had an endoscopic ultrasound, but both showed nothing unusual. “The doctor said, ‘Let’s remove your gallbladder to see if that’s the issue,’” Jackson recalls. When the surgery didn’t help, she was prescribed Norco, an opioid, to help her push through the pain so she could take care of her newborn and her older child and get back to her job. But by the time her daughter was 8 months old, the pain had broken through the medication, prompting a dash to the emergency room during a business trip in Florida. A weeklong hospitalization — and yet another MRI with contrast — finally revealed that Jackson had a type of pancreatic cancer called acinar cell carcinoma and that it was blocking one of her bile ducts.

The cancer had been missed on at least five imaging tests over ten months — an all-too-common occurrence because it is exceedingly difficult to visualize pancreatic cancer with current screening technology. About 40 percent of pancreatic tumors less than two centimeters in size are missed on CT scans, according to a 2021 study published in European Radiology. When patients turn up at the hospital suffering from a constellation of symptoms that could be signs of many diagnoses, it’s not unusual for busy ER radiologists to miss pancreatic abnormalities. In 2022, Michael B. Wallace, an interventional endoscopist from the Mayo Clinic in Jacksonville, Florida, conducted a study to determine just how often pancreatic cancer could be missed or go unrecognized when doctors order imaging to look for more likely diagnoses, such as kidney stones, appendicitis, and gallbladder infections. In examining CT scans and MRIs from one month to three years before pancreatic-cancer patients were diagnosed, Wallace discovered that as many as half of the scans indicated an abnormality in the pancreas that could have prompted more testing.
After hearing her diagnosis, Jackson says, her gastroenterologist could barely look her in the eye: “He was so heartbroken. He was like, ‘I must’ve missed something. How could this happen?’”

These kinds of misses are a major reason pancreatic cancer is projected to be the second deadliest in the United States by 2030. Only 12 to 15 percent of patients survive it because it is too often found too late. Approximately 67,530 people will be diagnosed with pancreatic cancer this year, with Black Americans, like Jackson, more likely to develop pancreatic cancer than any other group, according to the National Cancer Institute SEER data.

But recently, those who study the disease have found themselves cautiously optimistic. Part of this is due to the FDA’s approval of a highly effective daily pill (daraxonrasib) for metastatic pancreatic cancer, an event that grabbed headlines over the summer. But the positivity also stems from less publicized but still significant advances in early pancreatic-cancer detection. Over the past few years, researchers have been harnessing AI to develop new screenings that flag concerning or cancerous lesions on scans before they’re visible to the human eye. There is already promising data on this technology, and experts say the long-term results have the potential to be transformative.

Ajit Goenka, M.D., a specialist in nuclear medicine and abdominal imaging at the Mayo Clinic in Minnesota, has had to break pancreatic-cancer diagnoses to scores of patients who had previously received seemingly normal results on abdominal imaging — an experience that always leaves him both frustrated and ashamed on behalf of his profession. Every day, his team notices subtle signs of pancreatic cancer on imaging that should have aroused suspicion months, if not years, before. “The first time 80 to 85 percent of people hear pancreas cancer, they have unfortunately already lost the battle,” he says. “We need to be able to find it at a stage where we can flip that equation from 85 percent of patients presenting too late, to about 85 percent presenting at a stage where a curative treatment, like surgery, could be a part of the equation.”

Knowing pancreatic cancer can lie in wait on a cellular level for years before becoming symptomatic or detectable on imaging, Goenka set out to determine whether AI could sift through CT images to detect easy-to-miss signs of cancerous tumors, neoplasms (abnormal tissue growths), or precancerous cells. “AI is very good at looking at grains of sand, whereas we as human beings are better at looking at the beach,” Goenka explains.

He built an AI framework called REDMOD, which stands for radiomics-based early-detection model, training it with both CT scans taken from patients who were diagnosed with pancreatic cancer between three and 36 months after their scans and with control scans from healthy patients spanning approximately 15 years of clinical practice at the Mayo Clinic. By analyzing subtle patterns in the brightness and texture of the pancreas that are difficult for the human eye to appreciate, REDMOD can spot and flag subtle signs of cancer roughly 16 months earlier and at nearly double the rate of specialist radiologists. “You could ask ChatGPT to, in one minute, read a thousand-page book and find the page that says ‘red bird,’ but if I ask you, a human, to read a thousand-page book and, in retrospect, ask you to tell me the page that says ‘red bird,’ that’s hard to do,” says Wallace. It took months for imaging to verify Jackson’s metaphorical “red bird,” while solutions like Goenka’s REDMOD could have done it in minutes. If it had been available to her care team, she might still have her gallbladder.

Like Goenka, Neil Marya, M.D., has a memory bank full of frustrating and heartbreaking patient conversations. He is the co-director of the program in digital medicine at UMass Chan Medical School, and he says he struggled to tell patients that even though their biopsies came back negative, they still had a high chance of having cancer in their bile ducts because the biopsies are not sensitive enough to detect early disease. “It’s really awful,” he says, referring to how much anxiety this uncertainty sparks in his patients. Even worse, by the time his patients’ biopsies turned positive, it was often too late to remove the cancer or the organ.

Marya turned to AI to develop a way to accurately flag bile-duct lesions that are visibly suspicious or cancerous and are likely to come back with a negative biopsy. Using video data from previous endoscopies, Marya created an AI-based tool for cholangioscopies (the bile-duct equivalent of an endoscopy) that can analyze bile ducts for suspicious changes in real time. Along with his childhood friend Patrick Powers, a medical-application developer at UMass, Marya trained an AI tool (built using hardware from Nintendo Switch) to recognize various types of tumors and suspicious lesions he often spots during cholangioscopies by feeding it 20,000 random images from 130 procedures conducted at UMass and the Mayo Clinic. The fruit of his labor is SMART-AI, a plug-and-play hard drive that works with existing cholangioscope machines to visualize early cancerous growths better than biopsies do. A study Powers and Marya conducted in April 2026 suggested SMART-AI was remarkably effective; its first human trial was 88 percent accurate in diagnosing bile-duct cancer, compared with regular biopsies that were only 67 percent accurate.

For many cancers, preventive screening is a universal recommendation because current imaging is highly effective in catching disease early. The American Cancer Society recommends that women over age 45 with an average risk of breast cancer receive mammograms each year and that high-risk women over age 30 receive both an MRI and a mammogram. ACS also recommends colonoscopy screenings for anyone over age 45, and the Centers for Disease Control recommends that all former heavy smokers and people over 50 receive low-dose CT scans to screen for lung cancer. At this time, preventive screening for pancreatic cancer is incredibly targeted (reserved only for those who have relatives with a pancreatic-cancer diagnosis or who test positive for a high-risk gene mutation, or both). According to Dr. Vineet Syan Rolston and Dr. Mengmeng Du, both at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center, this is largely because pancreatic cancer is rare and screening wouldn’t necessarily find the cancer anyway. Currently, screening for high-risk patients at MSK includes blood tests and annual imaging that alternates between a magnetic-resonance cholangiopancreatography (radiation-free imaging that gives detailed images of the pancreatic and bile ducts) and an endoscopic ultrasound, in which a thin, flexible tube is passed through the mouth so a small ultrasound camera can look at the pancreas up close. But Wallace sees these new AI tools as having the potential to simplify this process and expand it to a wider population. “These AI systems are quite accurate,” says Wallace. “You can imagine putting this software in the emergency department and just running it on every scan being done and saying, ‘Flag it if it looks like there might be early pancreas cancer.’”

In China, Xiaomeng Li, Ph.D., has been using AI to help doctors more accurately spot rare cancers in biopsy tissue. Her software framework, called PRET, scans digital images of tissue samples and flags potential cancers or other abnormalities; it could help less experienced doctors, or those in remote or small hospitals, diagnose patients faster and more accurately. Careful to mention that PRET isn’t meant to replace specialist expertise or stage cancer, Li, of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, is nonetheless enthusiastic about its use as a validation or verification tool. Thus far, PRET has yielded impressive results: It has a 98 percent accuracy rate, outperforming 11 pathologists on lymph-node metastasis detection.

How long it may be until AI becomes a standardized element of screening for cancer — or for any medical problem — remains to be seen, but lately, progress to that end has been swift and significant. Between January and June of this year, the FDA approved 135 out of 181 AI-enabled radiology devices for medical purposes. And for the past few years, a radiology company called RadNet has been providing enhanced breast-cancer detection, an AI-powered mammogram, to clinics in New York and New Jersey. In 2025, to improve predictions of whether a woman will develop breast cancer over the next five years, the FDA approved Clairity Breast, an AI-powered platform that works with standard mammograms. The company received $43 million in funding to roll out the technology throughout the nation over the next few years so that leading imaging centers and health systems can have access to it.

Wallace says it took around three years for GI Genius, an AI-driven tool he helped develop to flag potentially cancerous polyps during colonoscopies, to go from an idea to FDA approval. He’s now at work on a large clinical trial of Cyst-X, an MRI-based AI algorithm that can ferret out pancreatic cysts — one of the few identifiable precursors to pancreatic cancer. Marya and Powers are still trying to clear various regulatory hurdles before a version of SMART-AI can be plugged into cholangioscope machines, and Li and her team have begun testing PRET at one hospital in mainland China and hope to expand to more hospitals soon.

As for Goenka, he’s in the midst of a large clinical trial of REDMOD that he hopes will help more of his patients be diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in time to benefit from surgery. “Early pancreatic cancer can leave the pancreas looking nearly normal,” says Goenka. “AI may be able to detect subtle patterns that humans cannot reliably see. In that sense, I do think AI can help scale human excellence.”

When cancer cells learn to survive a drug designed to stop them, where do you turn next? A new study points to an unexpected possibility: a medicine used to treat parasitic worms.

Researchers combined the deworming medicine with a targeted lung cancer drug. In laboratory experiments, the pairing reduced resistant cancer-cell viability. In mice, tumors took longer to double in size with the combination than with either drug alone.
The idea was to find a weakness in cells that had learned to withstand treatment, then put that weakness under pressure.

"The exciting message is that drug resistance may not make cancer cells invulnerable; it may leave them with weaknesses that we can target," pharmacology researcher Shakta Mani Satyam of RAK Medical and Health Sciences University in the United Arab Emirates told ScienceAlert.
The study, published in PLOS ONE, paired gefitinib, a targeted cancer treatment, with mebendazole, a medicine used against parasitic worm infections.
It focused on one model of EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer that had become resistant to gefitinib.

EGFR is a protein that helps relay signals telling cells to grow. Certain genetic changes can keep those signals active, driving cancer-cell multiplication. Gefitinib blocks this protein, but resistant cells can find ways to keep growing.
The researchers wondered whether disrupting another part of those cells could make them more vulnerable.
Mebendazole interferes with tiny structures inside cells that help organize division and move materials around. These structures support essential processes that multiplying cells depend on.
"Our idea was to attack the cancer from two directions simultaneously," Satyam said.
"Gefitinib blocks the growth signal, while mebendazole disrupts the cell's internal machinery and increases stress associated with DNA replication."

Every dividing cell must copy its DNA. The team's reasoning was that disrupting both growth signaling and internal machinery might make it harder for resistant cells to cope with continued multiplication.
First, they tested the medicines on resistant human lung cancer cells.
After 72 hours, cell viability with gefitinib alone remained at about 93 percent of the untreated control level. A low concentration of mebendazole alone lowered it to approximately 80 percent.
Combining the two brought that laboratory measure down to about 38 percent.
A fivefold higher concentration of mebendazole alone reduced viability further, to around 30 percent.
The combination with the lower mebendazole concentration produced a reduction comparable to that of the higher concentration alone, according to the paper.

In the cell experiments, tests also detected DNA damage, including breaks in one or both strands. The researchers interpret the findings as consistent with increased stress associated with copying DNA.
Next came experiments in mice carrying tumors grown from the resistant human cells.

In a 40-day study with eight mice per treatment group, the median time for tumors to double in size was 6.2 days without treatment. Mebendazole alone extended it to 10.3 days, while gefitinib alone extended it to 15.5 days.
With both drugs, the doubling time reached 25 days.
However, the tumors were not eliminated, and the findings are preclinical. Results from one resistant cancer model cannot establish how other lung cancers would respond.

The researchers also cannot yet determine whether mebendazole reverses resistance to gefitinib or adds damage that makes resistant cells less able to survive. They did not formally quantify drug synergy or directly track how the DNA-copying machinery failed.
"Our findings suggest that the combination does more than simply add another source of damage, but we cannot yet say conclusively that it fully restores sensitivity to gefitinib," Satyam said.
Delivering enough medicine to a human tumor is another hurdle. Mebendazole's absorption after swallowing can vary, so effective drug exposure and dosing need further investigation.

The mice showed no sustained body-weight loss, but that alone cannot establish safety. Further experiments must examine effects on organs and healthy tissues, prolonged use, and interactions between the medicines.

Additional resistant cell lines and patient-derived tumor models are research priorities. Satyam said resistance to osimertinib, a newer EGFR-targeted treatment, is an important question for future research.
"We are encouraged by the results, but further preclinical validation and careful assessment of drug exposure and safety must come before any conclusions about its clinical potential," Satyam said.
The research has been published in PLOS ONE.
