General Assembly adopts pandemic declaration, but not by consensus

The General Assembly on Monday adopted a political declaration on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response, by 153 in favour to three against (Argentina, Israel and United States) with two abstentions (New Zealand and Paraguay).
The text was due to be approved by consensus at a high-level meeting on 25 September.
Objections from the United States and a few other States blocked that, pushing the issue back to the assembly.
Read the full political declaration here.
Chile’s representative summed up one prevailing view, saying that “no country, no matter how big it might be or how prepared it might be, can alone address a threat that knows no borders.”

The declaration is political and non-binding. It calls for stronger national, regional and international cooperation, guided by science, equity and respect for human rights, and it welcomes last year’s landmark adoption of the World Health Organization (WHO) Pandemic Agreement.

“WHO welcomes this strong commitment by UN Member States to continue working together on pandemic prevention, preparedness and response,” said World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus.

“The world has come a long way since COVID-19. We urge countries to now fulfil the commitments they have made – especially to finalize negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing system (PABS) annex, so the WHO Pandemic Agreement can be opened for signature, begin the process of ratification and enter into force as international law.”
The agreement cannot be opened for signature until Member States complete the annex on pathogen access and benefit-sharing – the system by which countries would share samples and genetic data.
Those that do so would receive a share of any resulting vaccines, treatments and diagnostics.
Talks have stalled amid a standoff between developing countries and some high-income European nations together with the US.
The World Health Assembly – comprising the WHO’s 194 members – is due to return to the annex next May.
The US representative had previously cited “divisive ideologies that lack definitional consensus” as well as the declaration’s references to the continuing annex negotiations.

In addition to adopting the pandemic declaration, the 193-member world body had a number of items on its agenda on Monday, including the consideration of draft resolutions on the UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise and a political declaration of the high-level meeting to mark the 25th anniversary of the adoption of the anti-racism Durban Declaration and Programme of Action.
WHO aims to spot new outbreaks within 24 hours
The World Health Organization (WHO) on Monday launched a five-year strategy for its Hub for Pandemic and Epidemic Intelligence, with the goal of detecting emerging health threats within 24 hours.

Set up in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic, the hub wants every country to be able to identify and understand new threats quickly, so outbreaks can be contained before they become epidemics or spread internationally.
Colombia peace deal must endure as insecurity grows, Security Council hears

Nearly 10 years after Colombia signed a historic peace agreement to end a decades-long insurgency, the deal is under strain from growing insecurity – and the UN’s top official in the country says it cannot be allowed to falter.

Miroslav Jenča told the Security Council on Monday that the 2016 accord must be implemented in full, with proper funding, better coordination between institutions and protection for former combatants.

He pointed to real gains: rural development, and mechanisms for transitional justice and reparation for victims. But he admitted that implementation has had “many shortcomings” and that much remains to be done.
Security policy and the peace agreement should reinforce each other, Mr. Jenča said, and the accord should be carried out comprehensively.

“We look forward to the further definition of its policies, and we stand ready to support the Government in this regard,” he said, offering the experience gained by the UN Verification Mission over almost a decade of supporting implementation.

Communities in conflict-affected regions remain exposed to armed groups, geographical isolation and limited access to public services. Child recruitment, particularly among ethnic communities, and threats and attacks against women remain major concerns, ambassadors heard.
Government data presented to legislators show that illegal armed groups grew from around 15,000 members in 2022 to approximately 28,000 today.
Mr. Jenča also condemned the killings of civil society leaders María Ovidia Palechor and James Flor in Cauca on 1 September, highlighting the risks faced by rights defenders.
He said expanding economic opportunities, improving public services and strengthening local institutions were essential to reducing violence.
Despite these challenges, more than 11,000 former members of the FARC-EP rebel group remain committed to reintegration.
With State and international support, they have developed around 6,000 productive projects and 300 cooperatives in sectors including agriculture, tourism, trade and textiles.
Mr. Jenča highlighted tourism initiatives involving former combatants and victims, aimed at stimulating local economies and job markets.
However, economic sustainability and security remain significant challenges. Since the agreement was signed in 2016, 501 former combatants have been killed, most recently on 22 September in Cesar.

The Special Representative reaffirmed the UN mission's readiness to continue supporting implementation and highlighted its value on the ground, noting that over almost a decade it had built relationships of trust in some of regions most impacted by continuing violence.
Colombia had entered “a new political chapter, with wide ranging challenges ahead,” Mr. Jenča said, calling for “sustained international engagement in order to overcome remaining obstacles.”

DURANGO, Colo., Oct. 5, 2026 — Agile Space Industries today announced that Jonathan Baliff has joined its Board of Directors, bringing extensive experience in aerospace, finance, and corporate leadership. His appointment, alongside the addition of Theo Squires as Director of Strategy & Corporate Development, strengthens Agile’s ability to execute its long-term growth strategy, support capital formation, and pursue strategic opportunities as the company continues to scale.

Agile is entering its next phase with growing opportunities across the commercial and national security space. Jonathan Baliff Joins Board of Directors

Baliff brings extensive experience across aerospace, finance, and corporate leadership. A former U.S. Air Force aviator and engineer, he currently serves as an operating partner at Genesis Park, where he played a central role in the formation and financing of Redwire Corporation and later served as its chief financial officer. He previously served as president and CEO of Bristow Group and held senior leadership positions at NRG Energy and Credit Suisse. His experience raising capital, guiding strategic investments, and leading organizations through periods of growth and transformation will support Agile as the company continues to scale.

“Agile has proven it has the technology and operational expertise to compete, win, and profitably grow in a rapidly evolving space market,” said Baliff. “Our customers and capital providers will partner with us as we scale Agile’s technology, expand capacity, and efficiently deploy capital to support the company’s growth. Expanding Corporate Development to Support Long-Term Strategy

Squires serves as Agile’s Director of Strategy & Corporate Development. He also worked at Boston Consulting Group, advising advanced manufacturing companies on strategy and operations. At Agile, his experience supports capital formation, strategic investments and potential acquisitions of complementary technologies and capabilities to support the company’s broader growth strategy.

“Scaling advanced propulsion hardware requires both technical innovation and a disciplined approach to capital investment,” said Squires. “Our focus is on building a financial foundation to support higher-rate production while identifying strategic opportunities that complement Agile’s existing capabilities. They don't produce anything like the torrent of "shooting stars" associated with August's Perseids or December's Geminids, but the Taurid meteor showers have something else going for them — fireballs.

The Taurids are famous for occasionally producing exceptionally bright, slow-moving meteors that can streak dramatically across the night sky from September to December. As a bonus, they're visible from both the Northern and Southern hemispheres. That's because they appear to emanate from the constellation Taurus, which sits close to the ecliptic, the apparent path the sun takes across the sky as Earth orbits around it.

The Taurids are actually two closely related showers — the Southern Taurids and Northern Taurids — whose activity overlaps in late October and November. That's why they're known informally by skywatchers as the "Halloween fireballs." The broad overlapping peaks make the Taurids less about watching on one particular night and more about keeping an eye on the night sky for several weeks. Both have their radiant points — the place in the night sky where their "shooting stars" appear to come from — close to the famous Pleiades (M45) open cluster of stars in the constellation Taurus.
There's another tempting reason to watch the Taurids in 2026 — moonlight will cause little interference around the main peaks.

The Southern Taurids are already underway. According to the American Meteor Society, they're active from Sept. 20 through Nov. 20, with two distinct components. The annual component peaks around Oct. 14, while a component particularly associated with fireballs peaks overnight on Nov. 4-5. That's the night to circle if you're hoping to see one of the "Halloween Fireballs."

However, don't expect a conventional meteor storm. The Southern Taurids have an average zenithal hourly rate of about five meteors per hour. ZHR describes how many meteors an observer could theoretically see under ideal conditions with the shower's radiant directly overhead. In practice, observers see fewer, so this is not a chance to gather friends for a special show, as with the Perseids.

What the Southern Taurids lack in quantity, however, they can make up for in quality. Their meteors strike Earth's atmosphere at about 17 miles (27 kilometers) per second. That's relatively slow for a meteor, helping make some Taurids conspicuous as they travel across the sky. You don't see a Taurid meteor; you watch it.

If clouds allow, conditions should be favorable around Nov. 4-5. The moon will be absent most of the night, rising a couple of hours before dawn as a 17%-illuminated waning crescent — too dim to affect visibility of meteors.
The Northern Taurids begin later, becoming active on Oct. 20 and continuing through Dec. 10, according to the American Meteor Society. They're expected to peak overnight on Nov. 11-12.

Once again, rates are low — around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions — but fireballs are possible. Northern Taurid meteors enter the atmosphere at around 18 miles (29 km) per second, similarly as slow as their southern counterparts.

Observing conditions at the peak should be excellent. The moon will be a slender 5%-illuminated waxing crescent and will be practically absent from the night sky overnight on Nov. 11-12, leaving the night dark.

The distinction between the two Taurid showers isn't particularly important if you're simply outside hoping to see a fireball. In late October and early November, both streams are active at the same time, potentially producing around 10 Taurids per hour under clear, moon-free conditions.
Why are Taurids called the 'Halloween Fireballs'?

The nickname comes partly from timing. Their maxima are also broad rather than sharp. According to EarthSky, the Taurids tend to "ramble along" over the period, becoming particularly noticeable when the two branches overlap from late October into early November — Halloween.
It's also a reference to their tendency to produce fireballs, exceptionally bright meteors caused when larger pieces of space debris plunge into Earth's atmosphere.

Some years are considerably better for Taurid fireballs than others, and it's impossible to tell for sure in advance. EarthSky notes that enhanced displays occurred in 2008, 2015 and 2022, when Earth encountered concentrations of larger debris within the stream. However, don't expect a repeat in 2026 — the next predicted Taurid fireball swarm isn't expected until 2032.
That doesn't mean there won't be fireballs this year, only that an unusually high number isn't predicted.

Both Taurid meteor showers are linked to Comet 2P/Encke, a three-mile-wide (4.8-kilometer) comet that circles the sun every 3.25 years — the shortest known cometary orbit, according to NASA. However, the Taurids belong to a much larger complex of dust, rocks, comets and asteroids, possibly created when a much bigger object fragmented thousands of years ago. Each fall, Earth crosses different parts of this sprawling debris stream, producing the overlapping Northern and Southern Taurids and, occasionally, the larger fragments that create spectacular fireballs.

Both showers appear to originate from Taurus, a constellation that rises during the evening and climbs higher into the sky as the night progresses. Around midnight, Taurus is well placed for many observers.

However, there's no need to find Taurus. Meteors can appear anywhere in the sky, and staring directly at the radiant can actually mean seeing shorter meteor trails. The best advice is to treat the period as a great time for naked-eye stargazing, with the usual rules applying — find somewhere away from bright lights with as wide a view of the sky as possible, and give your eyes about 20 minutes to adjust to the darkness. Binoculars and telescopes will restrict your field of view and make meteor watching impossible.

Above all, be patient. The Taurids are a slow burn in every sense — low rates, slow-moving meteors and weeks of activity. But if one of those meteors happens to be a brilliant fireball, it could easily be one of the most memorable "shooting stars" you see all year.

On Oct. 12, 1964, the Soviet Union launched Voskhod 1, a 24-hour crewed mission that achieved several "firsts" for human spaceflight. This was the first time that a spacecraft carried more than one person into orbit, with three cosmonauts packed inside the spacecraft.

Only two cosmonauts were originally supposed to fly on this mission, but Soviet politicians pressured the Russian space program to add one more. This left no room for spacesuits on board, so this also became the first spaceflight without spacesuits.
Two of the crewmembers, an engineer and a doctor, became the first civilians to go to space.

Voskhod 1 served as yet another first for the Soviet Union during a space race kicked off by the launch of Sputnik 1 in 1957 and followed up by the first human spaceflight with Yuri Gagarin in 1961. And while the United States did follow up with its one human spaceflights, until Oct. 12, 1964, every mission had one person on board.

That changed with Voskhod 1, which crammed three man into a spacecraft not much larger than the Soviet Union's one-person Vostok spacecraft. At the time, NASA was develoing the two-person Gemini spacecraft, which prompted the Soviet Union's then leader to push for an edge.

"Soviet leader [Nikita] Khrushchev contacted Korolev and ordered him to convert the Vostok spacecraft into a vehicle capable of carrying not two, but three cosmonauts," according to space historian Asif Siddiqi, referring to Sergei Korolev, chief designer of the Soviet space program.

In order to fit a three people inside, the Voskhod 1 cosmonauts - commander Vladimir Komarov and his crew Konstantin Feoktistov and Boris Yegorov - did not wear spacesuits traditionally used for launch and landing, adding substantial risk to the flight. They also stayed inside their spacecraft when it landed, unlike Vostok crews like Gagarin, who parachuted out of them after reentry.
The Voskhod 1 mission lasted just over 24 hours, during which its crew performed experimented with the behavior of liquids and gases in microgravity and photographed the Earth.
NASA's first multi-crew mission, Gemini 3, would launch about six month later on March 23, 1965.

A neon blue pool swirls amongst what look like clouds, all surrounded by a bright red stretch of land. This might look like the surface of an alien planet, but it's actually a salt flat right here on Earth, seen from space.
Etosha National Park in northern Namibia hosts the largest salt pan, or piece of land covered with salt and other minerals, in the country.
This image of the Etosha Pan was captured on April 5 of this year by Europe's Copernicus Sentinel-2 mission, which consists of two identical satellites in the same orbit.
The Sentinel-2 pair observe and capture imagery of our planet in different wavelengths using a high-resolution multispectral imager that can see 13 different spectral bands, or ranges of wavelengths.

By looking at our planet from space, and observing it through different wavelengths and colors, we can better understand Earth's topography and how it changes over time. With this image, researchers can better understand this landmark in Namibia, a nation in southwestern Africa.
While this image is strikingly beautiful, the Etosha Pan doesn't exactly look like this in real life. If you were standing close to the pan in the national park, it would look bright white.
While this is a real image, false color has been added, which allows scientists to separate different types of vegetation and topography.

With the false color, the vegetation surrounding the salt pan appears in shades of red, while the salt pan itself looks like a mix of bright, light and dark blues with cloudy sediment floating around.

The varied vegetation captured in this false-color image includes grassland, savannas and mopane trees, which appear bright red. These trees are not only a dominant type of vegetation in areas of this park, they also provide essential shelter and habitats for local wildlife, including elephants, giraffe and leopards.

Scientists discover vanillaâs hidden healing potential
Researchers have uncovered surprising healing potential in vanilla, revealing that its signature flavor compound could help fight infections, reduce inflammation, and improve wound care.

- Scientists have discovered that vanillin, the compound that gives vanilla its distinctive flavor, has powerful properties that could help fight infections, reduce inflammation, and promote wound healing. The inexpensive, widely available ingredient could one day become an important component of advanced wound treatments and regenerative medicine.

The compound responsible for vanilla's familiar sweet flavor and aroma could have an unexpected future in medicine. Scientists at Flinders University have identified properties in vanillin that could make it a promising ingredient in treatments for chronic wounds, infections, and damaged tissue.

Researchers from the university's Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory found that vanillin has notable antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and antibacterial properties. Together, these effects could make the compound useful in developing wound care products that address several challenges associated with healing.

Vanillin is the main flavor and fragrance compound found in natural vanilla pods. It can also be manufactured synthetically using materials derived from sources such as clove oil or rice. Although best known for giving foods their distinctive vanilla flavor, the molecule has chemical properties that could make it valuable far beyond the kitchen.
How Vanilla's Chemistry Could Help Heal Wounds

Vanillin is more than just a flavoring ingredient. Its molecular structure allows it to interact with other substances in ways that could be useful for medicine, particularly in materials designed to protect wounds and deliver treatments.

For example, vanillin can function as a dynamic crosslinker, helping connect different components within a material. This ability could make it useful in creating specialized medical formulations, including materials that carry drugs or support tissue repair.

The Flinders researchers examined vanillin through a framework that connects familiar food ingredients with practical medical applications. Their work explores how the same chemical characteristics that make vanillin useful in everyday products could also contribute to biological effects that benefit human health.

"Vanillin is among the most widely used flavor compounds in the global food system, valued for its sensory attributes, chemical stability and long history of safety - and that can be transferred to other areas, such as medical uses," says Professor Krasimir Vasilev, Professor of Biomedical Nanotechnology at Flinders University and Director of Flinders' Biomedical Nanoengineering Laboratory.
A Potential New Treatment for Chronic Wounds and Ulcers

One particularly promising application involves chronic wounds and ulcers, which can be difficult to treat because of persistent inflammation, bacterial contamination, and damage caused by oxidative stress.

Oxidative stress occurs when harmful reactive molecules overwhelm the body's protective defenses, potentially damaging cells and interfering with tissue repair. A material capable of addressing oxidative stress, inflammation, and bacteria could therefore offer several advantages in wound care.

"Because vanillin's synthetic form is abundant and cost-effective, we believe vanillin-based formulations may offer safe and multifunctional solutions for ulcer treatment and targeted drug delivery, especially of hydrophobic compounds.

"Owing to its amphiphilic molecular structure, vanillin can interact with reactive oxygen species, cellular membranes, and polymeric matrices, providing a basis for its incorporation into functional formulations."

Hydrophobic compounds are substances that do not dissolve easily in water, a characteristic that can make certain medications difficult to formulate and deliver effectively. Vanillin's chemical structure may help researchers design materials that carry these compounds to where they are needed.

Although the findings highlight intriguing possibilities, vanillin-based wound treatments would still need further development and clinical testing before their effectiveness and safety in patients could be established.
From Peppermint Oil to Advanced Medical Coatings
The investigation into vanillin builds on a broader effort at Flinders University to uncover useful medical properties in everyday food ingredients.

In February 2026, the research team published related work in the journal Small, describing a medical coating developed from peppermint oil. The coating, created at the nanoscale, was designed to protect against bacterial infection, inflammation, and oxidative stress while remaining compatible with human tissue.
Because the coating can be applied to medical materials, it could provide a way to introduce several protective functions into products used in healthcare.
Surprisingly, the inspiration for this research came from a simple personal experience.

Professor Vasilev noticed that eating peppermint leaves from his drink significantly eased his sore throat. Curious about the possible biological explanation, he began investigating whether the beneficial properties of peppermint could be incorporated into a durable protective coating.

That idea led him to explore the use of plasma technology, a field he has studied for more than 20 years. Plasma processing can be used to modify material surfaces and create thin functional coatings, potentially allowing biologically active compounds to be incorporated into medical products.
The work with peppermint helped establish an approach that researchers are now extending to vanillin.
Why Vanillin Could Be Especially Useful for Future Medicine
Vanillin offers another important advantage beyond its potential biological activity: it is inexpensive and readily available.

Because synthetic vanillin can be produced in large quantities, researchers believe it could be easier to incorporate into commercially manufactured medical products than some more expensive or difficult-to-source compounds.
Its relatively simple molecular structure and compatibility with established manufacturing processes could also support consistent product quality, reliable supplies, and large-scale production.
These practical considerations are especially important when moving a promising scientific concept from the laboratory toward real medical applications.

The researchers envision vanillin eventually becoming an ingredient in advanced wound dressings, ulcer treatments, targeted drug delivery systems, and therapies designed to support tissue regeneration.

"With coordinated engagement between academia, clinicians, and industry, vanillin has the potential to progress from an underutilized bioactive to a clinically deployable component of next-generation wound care and regenerative therapeutics," says Professor Vasilev.

The findings suggest that a compound commonly associated with desserts and sweet fragrances could eventually contribute to an entirely different field: helping scientists develop better ways to protect damaged tissue and support healing.

The study, "Vanillin as a bioactive component in biomedical formulations for chronic wound healing and tissue regeneration," was conducted by Borislav Stoilov, Vi Khanh Truong, Christopher Delaney, and Krasimir Vasilev. It was published in the International Journal of Pharmaceutics.

Just 10 minutes of daily exercise could unlock deeper sleep

- Getting better sleep might be as simple as moving a little more every day. Researchers at The University of Texas at Austin found that people who exercised more frequently experienced more deep, restorative sleep, which is essential for brain recovery, memory, and emotional well-being. Surprisingly, just 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous exercise per day was associated with measurable benefits, while even light activities like walking and standing breaks were linked to better sleep and mood.

What if getting better sleep depends not just on how much you exercise, but how often you move? Research from The University of Texas at Austin suggests that being physically active every day, even for short periods, may help people spend more time in the deep, restorative stages of sleep that support recovery, mood, and mental health.

The findings suggest that consistency could be an important but often overlooked part of the relationship between exercise and sleep. Rather than saving all their workouts for the weekend, people may benefit from making movement a regular part of their daily routines.

The study, published in the Journal of Physical Activity & Health, examined activity and sleep data collected from University of Texas students who wore Fitbit devices over several months. While previous studies have largely examined how much time people spend exercising, the researchers focused on a different question: Does the number of days someone exercises influence how well they sleep?

"We wanted to know whether it matters if someone spreads out their exercise over the week versus doing it all at once, like a 'weekend warrior,'" said Benjamin Baird, a research assistant professor of psychology in UT Austin's College of Liberal Arts. "And for sleep health, frequency does seem to matter."
Just 10 Minutes of Daily Exercise May Improve Deep Sleep

The researchers found that participants who exercised more frequently tended to experience more restorative sleep. The findings build on previous research connecting physical activity with non-REM sleep, a stage that includes the deep sleep essential for physical recovery and healthy brain function.

Chris Corral, who recently earned a master's degree in health behavior and health education from UT Austin and co-led the study, explained that deep sleep is especially important during the early hours of the night. During this period, the body carries out many of the processes that help it recover from the day's physical and mental demands.
Participants who were active more often spent more time in these valuable stages of sleep.
"That's exactly what you want," Baird said.
"Better sleep means better brain health and potentially lower risks of chronic disease and depression."

One particularly encouraging finding was how little exercise appeared to be necessary. Among the young adults studied, as little as 10 minutes of moderate to vigorous physical activity per day was associated with better sleep.

That level of effort does not require an exhausting workout. According to the researchers, moderate to vigorous activity involves breathing harder than usual while still being able to carry on a conversation. On a scale of 1 to 10, the effort would feel like approximately a 6.

Even gentler movement appeared to offer benefits. Regular walking and taking breaks from sitting to stand were also associated with healthier sleep patterns and a more positive mood the following day.
Better Sleep Linked to Improved Mood and Energy
The potential benefits extended beyond what happened during the night. Participants who exercised more regularly also tended to feel more energetic and experience less stress the next day.
"We saw that more non-REM sleep was tied to better next-day mood and energy," Baird noted.

This connection is important because sleep affects far more than whether someone feels rested in the morning. Deep sleep helps the brain and body recover, supporting processes involved in memory, emotional regulation, and overall health.

Previous research has repeatedly linked physical activity with improved sleep, while better sleep itself is associated with greater well-being. However, many earlier investigations took place in controlled laboratories and examined relatively brief periods, sometimes measuring the effects of exercise over a single night.
The UT Austin team wanted to understand how these relationships played out under ordinary living conditions, where exercise habits, sleep schedules, and daily activities can vary considerably.

To accomplish this, the researchers used wearable fitness trackers to collect information over several months. The Fitbit data allowed them to compare participants' movement habits with their sleep patterns over time, offering a more detailed picture of how everyday activity relates to sleep quality and next-day mood.
Although the findings reveal meaningful associations, the observational approach does not establish that exercising more frequently directly causes improvements in sleep.
Why Daily Exercise May Be Better Than Weekend Workouts
The results also raise questions about how people should organize their exercise routines.

Current recommendations from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the World Health Organization call for approximately 150 minutes of moderate physical activity each week. However, those recommendations do not require people to distribute their activity evenly across the seven days.
For some, meeting a weekly exercise target means taking long walks or completing challenging workouts on Saturday and Sunday. Others prefer shorter sessions spread throughout the week.

The UT Austin findings suggest that the second approach may offer particular advantages for sleep, although more research is needed to determine whether daily activity is better than completing an equivalent amount of exercise on fewer days.
"Our results suggest that daily movement may be better for sleep than doing it all on the weekend," Corral said.
If further studies confirm the importance of exercise frequency, the findings could eventually influence how public health organizations advise people to stay active.
"Current guidelines don't reflect the importance of frequency for sleep health," Baird said. "Having this kind of data allows us to start thinking about whether they should."
What Better Sleep Could Mean for Brain Health
The possible implications go well beyond feeling more alert after waking up.

During sleep, the brain performs essential maintenance functions, including strengthening memories and removing waste products that accumulate during waking hours. Healthy sleep is also closely connected with emotional well-being and long-term physical health.
"Sleep is when your brain stores memories, clears waste and resets," Corral explained. "Better sleep means better brain health and potentially lower risks of chronic disease and depression."
The research is part of UT Austin's Whole Communities -- Whole Health initiative, an interdisciplinary program that works with communities to investigate factors influencing health and well-being.

The team is now preparing to examine whether the same patterns appear in a larger and more diverse population through the Whole Communities -- Whole Health five-year cohort study. This next phase will help researchers determine whether the findings extend beyond college students to people of different ages and physical activity levels.
For now, the results point toward an accessible way to potentially improve sleep: Make physical activity a regular part of everyday life.

Rather than focusing exclusively on long workouts or ambitious fitness goals, people may benefit from finding small opportunities to move throughout the day. A brief exercise session, a walk, or simply getting up regularly instead of remaining seated may all contribute to healthier routines.
"You don't need to run marathons," Corral said. "Just moving a little each day helps. Light activity counts too. Doing something is better than doing nothing."
Materials provided by University of Texas at Austin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Drones watching for sharks off Australia's east coast have filmed dozens of young hammerheads swimming together in shallow water near popular beaches.

In southeast Queensland, researchers recorded groups of up to 80 scalloped hammerhead sharks at Burleigh Beach on the Gold Coast. Farther north, at Noosa Main Beach on the Sunshine Coast, the largest group contained an estimated 100.
Several years of drone records showed where these young sharks gathered and when the biggest groups appeared. The researchers say these stretches of coast may be important habitat for juveniles.
Shark researcher Maddison Cross, affiliated with the University of the Sunshine Coast and Queensland's Department of Primary Industries, led the study.

The team used records from Queensland's SharkSmart program, which flies drones near beaches to monitor sharks for public safety. The flights also record animals moving through coastal waters, allowing scientists to study them without catching or handling them.

Researchers analyzed data from 20,911 flights at nine beaches between September 2020 and December 2024. They identified 84 occasions when scalloped hammerheads were seen, totaling 2,696 shark observations. Some animals were probably recorded more than once, so this is not a count of distinct individuals.
Most observations came from Burleigh and Noosa, where hammerheads usually appeared in groups. At other beaches, they were generally alone or in pairs.

The largest gatherings occurred in April, May, and June, during Australia's autumn and early winter. At Burleigh, groups repeatedly used waters near the rocky headland at the beach's southern end. Recorded movement paths overlapped in 2023 and 2024.

From above, the team could map where groups gathered and compare their movements across beaches. Larger hammerheads off North Stradbroke Island generally followed straighter coastal routes, while juveniles at Burleigh and Noosa used smaller areas.

Across the full dataset, estimated shark length averaged about 1.09 meters (3.6 feet). Most of the sharks at those two sites were juveniles. Estimated sizes pointed to a mix of animals in their first year and others around one to two years old.
They were not newborn pups, and the researchers could not confirm that these beaches met the criteria for nursery grounds.

The researchers propose that the sites may give young sharks somewhere to feed or shelter. Nearby reefs and rocky areas could support prey, and swimming together might help juveniles avoid predators. Why they gather remains unclear.

Researchers could not reliably recognize individual sharks, so they cannot establish whether the same animals returned each year or how long they stayed. At Noosa, gatherings recorded in 2023 were not seen during the corresponding period in 2024. The researchers note that changes in habitat use or water clarity could explain the difference, since murky water makes sharks harder to detect.
Scalloped hammerheads have suffered steep population declines and are classified globally as critically endangered.
Both gathering sites are covered by Queensland's shark-control program. Burleigh uses shark nets, while Noosa uses nets and baited drumlines to reduce shark-bite risk.

Government records cited in the study show that the program caught 675 scalloped hammerheads statewide between 2001 and 2024. All but 10 were dead. At Burleigh and Noosa combined, 63 were caught in nets and two on drumlines, including both juveniles and adults.

The study notes that captures of juvenile sharks under 120 centimeters peak from September to February, while drone surveys recorded gatherings from March to June. The team suggests this difference may reflect young sharks moving from sheltered nursery areas into more exposed coastal waters as they grow.

Some groups temporarily split apart when snorkelers or paddleboarders approached, although these encounters were not systematically measured. The researchers list keeping a distance from the groups and avoiding chasing or surrounding the sharks among possible measures to reduce disturbance.
They also call for longer-term monitoring, including tracking individuals with acoustic tags, to establish how these coastal sites connect with nearby nursery habitats.
The research has been published in Marine Biology.
For people with inflammatory bowel disease, feeling better on treatment doesn't always mean a permanent improvement – the disease can flare again.
A study suggests part of the explanation may lie in intestinal cells that stay fragile even when symptoms such as abdominal pain and diarrhea are controlled.
Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are the main forms of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). Both involve chronic inflammation of the digestive tract.
Treatment can bring IBD into remission, a period when its activity subsides, but another flare can follow.
Researchers found signs of abnormal cell death in gut tissue even from patients whose disease was under control.

"The bowel may still carry a vulnerability that is not apparent from symptoms alone," gastroenterologist Britt Christensen, head of the Inflammatory Bowel Disease Unit at the Royal Melbourne Hospital, told ScienceAlert.
The study, published in Science, examined more than 900 intestinal biopsies, small tissue samples, from 80 people with and without IBD. Most patients with IBD had inactive or mildly active disease.
Led by researchers at Australia's Walter and Eliza Hall Institute, the team investigated the intestinal lining: a protective layer that constantly rebuilds itself.
Normally, controlled cell death removes unwanted or damaged cells, while stem cells produce replacements.
The researchers found that inflammation could change how intestinal cells behave, making them more vulnerable to abnormal death signals.
Some signals were detectable even in tissue without obvious inflammation, hinting that problems could persist beneath an apparently healthy surface.
"This suggests that clinical remission does not always mean the underlying biology has returned to normal," Christensen explained.

To investigate further, the researchers grew miniature intestinal tissues from human samples. These laboratory models, called organoids, let scientists examine how cells respond to inflammation. Other researchers have used human cells to recreate features of IBD on a chip.

The experiments revealed an unexpected connection between two ways cells die. Patient tissue showed signals associated with necroptosis, a process that can rupture cells and release contents that promote inflammation.
But when organoids were exposed to inflammatory signals, their cells died mainly through apoptosis, a more orderly process of cellular dismantling.
Blocking necroptosis did not prevent cell death under the conditions tested. So drugs targeting a signal seen in diseased tissue may not be enough on their own to protect cells.
In the lab, deleting specific genes protected particular cell types. Further research is needed to determine whether these mechanisms can be safely targeted in patients.
The team examined whether the tissue findings were associated with later flares.

Of 52 patients with IBD, 30 had follow-up information covering two to three years. Sixteen experienced a flare requiring intensified or changed treatment, while 14 remained stable. Twenty-two were lost to follow-up.

Those who later relapsed had elevated levels of a cell-death signaling marker compared with people without IBD. However, that comparison doesn't establish whether the marker can tell who will relapse and who won't.

Patients who relapsed also had greater microscopic inflammation initially. Larger studies could potentially establish whether the signals provide useful information beyond existing inflammation measurements.
"The follow-up findings are promising but preliminary," Christensen cautioned.
For now, the findings may help explain why the disease keeps coming back, though they aren't a test doctors can use to predict a flare.
"Protecting the lining and its ability to regenerate could therefore complement treatments that control inflammation," Christensen said.
But cell-death pathways also serve essential functions, including removing damaged or potentially cancerous cells.
"We have not shown that blocking these mechanisms safely prevents flares in patients," Christensen said.

The longer-term goal is what she calls "molecular healing": addressing the cellular problems that persist beneath apparent recovery. Whether that can keep patients well for longer is yet to be tested.
The research has been published in Science.
Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup.

Some of the biggest stories in science last week were the announcement of the Nobel Prize awards in Chemistry, Physics, and Physiology or Medicine. So we’re going to focus on those groundbreaking research topics today—with a fun little animal story at the end to send us off, of course.

Let’s start with the prize for physiology or medicine, which was announced last Monday. This year’s award went to Karl Deisseroth at Stanford University, Peter Hegemann at Humboldt University of Berlin, and Georg Nagel at the University of Wurzburg in Germany. They were recognized for their discoveries around light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Optogenetics allows scientists to switch individual brain cells on and off. Because neurons use electrical signals to communicate with one another, scientists realized almost a century ago that they could use electrical stimulation to activate brain cells. Optogenetics combines this idea with genetic engineering to allow for more targeted, less invasive, safer cell stimulation than used to be possible. After genetically modifying neurons to make proteins that react to light, researchers can control those cells with a flash of light instead of an electrode.

Hegemann and Nagel contributed to the field by studying a single-celled alga that swims toward light, which they found had to do with a particular protein that opened up pores in the cell membrane when exposed to light. Deisseroth took those findings and applied them to experiments in living mammals.
We spoke to him about his win last week. Here he is explaining the impact of his discovery:

Karl Deisseroth: You know, once you know what matters for function, you can ask: How can dysfunction be addressed? You know, are there cells that cause dysfunction? Are there cells that can counteract dysfunction in a precise way? And what we're doing now is—and many others as well—is we're seeing: how can we leverage this precision to find new treatments, new medications, new neuromodulator approaches that build on this foundation of causality?

You know, this brings an opportunity that might help me communicate more with the public and to share the excitement of science, how discovery happens, how unlikely things get nurtured and that it takes time and it takes risk but that the outcome can be amazing if we’re willing to take the time and the risk.

Feltman: Last Tuesday saw Francis Halzen from the University of Wisconsin–Madison secure a rare solo award in Physics for the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of extraterrestrial origin. Here to tell us more about his contributions to the field is Joseph Howlett, a senior reporter at Scientific American and our resident physics expert. Tell us about those neutrinos, Joe!

Joseph Howlett: So neutrinos are my personal favorite fundamental particle. Of the 17 that we know about, the neutrinos are the ones we know the least. And that's why they've netted five times the Nobel Prize in Physics now.

The main thing that makes neutrinos different from other particles is that they pass through regular matter almost all the time without interacting. So there's neutrinos coming from space, from faraway black holes where super violent things are happening, like supernova and accretion, and these send out these very high-energy neutrinos. They make it all the way to Earth, but almost all the time they pass right through. We never notice that they're here. They're actually passing through us all the time. Neutrinos from the sun go right through our bodies without interacting.

It's really hard to build a detector that can catch a neutrino. And Halzen had this super ambitious idea to do so at the South Pole. He spearheaded the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. They chose Antarctica because it's a place with a lot of ice, and ice is great because when a neutrino interacts with ice, the light shines right through. It can go right through the ice like it's not there, all the way to whatever cameras you've buried inside.

So that was Halzen's great idea was that the Earth built this natural detector for us, right? All we have to do is put the cameras there to capture the light. So they bored these mile-deep holes with hot water jets and then lowered these strings of expensive cameras into each of them.

They span like a cubic kilometer of ice. And when a neutrino passes through that ice, usually it goes right through, but very rarely it will interact with one of the water molecules and produce a shower of light. And because the cameras are there, they can capture that light and say where that neutrino came from and how much energy it has.
So for the first time, we're able to see these neutrinos from these very, very faraway galaxies.

And actually, IceCube was the first experiment to see neutrinos from outer space, from outside of our solar system with this super high energy. So we've learned a lot about the universe thanks to this one experiment. It's also heralded this new era that astronomers call multimessenger astronomy. Basically, we've been looking at the sky with telescopes for hundreds of years, right? Measuring the light from faraway galaxies, from stars, X-rays even from black holes. But neutrinos are a whole new thing. They're not light. We're able to see the universe through a different lens. And when you combine this with the light measurements from all the telescopes in space and across the world, and you combine them additionally with gravitational wave detectors, which are another new technology that's won a Nobel Prize recently, now we have these three lenses that together can look at the same faraway objects and teach us all kinds of new things about them.

The thing about the multimessenger era is that it's just beginning. IceCube's only been operating for 16 years, and it's got a lot of life left to live, so we're gonna continue to learn all kinds of new things about the universe thanks to neutrinos, especially combined with these other experiments measuring light and gravitational waves.
Feltman: Thanks for breaking that down for us, Joe.

Last but not least is the Nobel Prize in Chemistry, which this year honored Henri Kagan of Paris-Sud University and Kenso Soai of the Tokyo University of Science for their pioneering research on autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis. Try saying that one five times fast!

Many molecules come in two versions that are mirror images of each other. They can’t be superimposed over one another, the same way you couldn’t lay your right and left hands on top of each other and get them to line up. That’s called chirality, which happens to be one of my favorite words. When chemists create chiral molecules in the lab, they typically end up with equal amounts of each version. But that's not ideal, because the proteins in your cells—and in the natural world in general—are made from only one of those mirror images. Kagan and Soai figured out how to create just one of those mirror images at a time.

We’ll wrap up today’s news roundup with a story about a very, very old tortoise. The oldest tortoise, in fact. And not just the oldest tortoise, but the oldest terrestrial animal known to man. His name? Jonathan.

Giant tortoises are known generally for their long lifespans, but at around 190 years old, Jonathan is at least a century older than seems to be standard for his kind. And yeah, he is definitely that old. Photographs have confirmed that he was fully mature when he was brought to the island of Saint Helena in 1882, which means he had to have been at least 50 at the time.

A study published last week in Science Advances aims to explain how Jonathan is still alive and kicking all these years later. Genetic analysis of the tortoise compared with four of his peers apparently revealed mutations associated with DNA repair, cancer, telomere maintenance, mitochondrial health, insulin regulation, and other pathways associated with aging.

The researchers also took a look at the methylation of Jonathan’s genome. Methylation is when a small chemical tag gets added to DNA, which generally serves to turn a gene off. One sign of aging is a process called methylation entropy, which is where random patterns of methylation start to become more common. In other words, your body gets worse at targeting the right genes to switch off, which makes it more likely that some important protein won’t get made the way it’s supposed to.

In Johnathan’s genome, methylation entropy was unusually low in gene regions associated with mitochondrial function, RNA processing, and genome repair. That could give scientists some clues about what genes to target if they want to increase lifespan for other animals.
Speaking of longevity: We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about why there’s so much shoddy science in this very buzzy field of research.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

Shares of Six Flags Entertainment plunged more than 10% in after-hours trading Monday following reports of a deadly roller coaster incident at one of its amusement parks in Georgia, marking a sharp reversal from gains during the regular session.
The stock had closed 4.5% higher during regular trading before the after-hours sell-off.

One person died and several others were injured in an incident involving the park's 200-foot-tall Goliath roller coaster at Six Flags Over Georgia in Cobb County shortly before 4 p.m. Monday, according to the report, citing local police.
Police did not provide additional details about the incident, the report showed.

Witnesses told a local news station they saw a man fall from the roller coaster and strike the ride several times. Riders were later seen being evacuated from the roller coaster after it stopped near the top of the ride, the report said.

Six Flags said its park staff and local authorities responded immediately to the incident, adding that it was cooperating fully with the investigation, had temporarily closed similar attractions across its parks and would not release further details out of respect for the family's privacy, according to the report.
The company's shares have fallen 22% year to date.

Asian technology stocks fell Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into regional markets, with worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition denting sentiment.

Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 8%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 6.7% — both hit their lowest levels since August.

In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.8%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares.

Tokyo Electron, a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 6.75%, while Advantest, which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 5.65%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell 4.94%, Disco lost 4.69% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.64%.

The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT, which reported progress on a new chip structure.

The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply.
Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates.
BANGKOK — The International Monetary Fund has raised its forecast for global economic growth this year as the AI-driven investment boom helps offset some of the impact from surging energy costs.
The IMF expects the global economy to grow at 3.1% in 2026, up from the 3% projected in July, but slower than the 3.5% rate last year. For 2027, it kept the forecast unchanged at 3.4%.

The UN agency expects inflation at 4.1% in 2027, above the 3.9% it projected in July – when it estimated the Strait of Hormuz would reopen by mid-July, with conditions broadly returning to pre-war levels by March 2027. For the current year, it maintained its 4.7% outlook.

The IMF now estimates that the Strait of Hormuz will reopen in March next year and return to pre-war state by October. Gulf crude exports averaged 88% of pre-conflict levels in September as traffic picked up, the international body said.

The report was released at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok this week, where finance ministers and central bank governors from the fund's 191 members are meeting to discuss geopolitical tensions, mounting public debt and artificial intelligence.

AI-related investment gave the global economy a "demand impulse" that helped activity in the first half of the year hold up better than expected, despite the Middle East war and trade tensions, the IMF said. Financial markets also stayed largely calm, which the fund said may partly reflect "AI-related exuberance."

For now, "use of buffers and adaptability have helped economies weather the negative shocks," the IMF said, citing measures such as diversifying fuel sources, tapping strategic reserves that have contained the energy-market turmoil unleashed by the Middle East war.

But that cushion is "rapidly narrowing" in the near term, it said. Global oil reserves are being drawn down by about 2.7 million barrels a day, nearing levels that could trigger sharp price moves, and energy constraints could impair the AI-led momentum. The growing unease over governments' fiscal health also adds to the headwinds.
Overall growth is also becoming increasingly uneven. Thirty-two economies now account for 95% of global growth, down from 54 in April.

Countries that have limited exposure to the war-led supply shock and are catering to the AI-led demand are holding up or strengthening. Taiwan is forecast to grow 10.7% this year and South Korea 3.3%, up from 1.1% in 2025 on semiconductor demand. The U.S. is projected to expand 2.3% in both 2026 and 2027, supported by private consumption, fiscal policy and tech investment.

Energy importers outside that tech supply chain face higher import bills, weaker real incomes and less fiscal room. The euro zone is estimated to eke out just 1.1% growth this year amid higher energy costs and weak consumer confidence. The Middle East and Central Asia is projected to contract 0.3% this year, with Bahrain, Iraq, Kuwait and Qatar facing double-digit declines before double-digit rebounds in 2027.

China is forecast to grow 4.5% this year and 4.0% in 2027, with higher oil prices and structural headwinds weighing on activity. Second-quarter growth of 4.3% was weaker than expected as sluggish consumption and property strains outweighed robust exports.

"The global economy is not simply slowing or accelerating; rather, growth is being reallocated across countries according to their exposure to the war-induced supply shock and AI-related demand strength," the IMF said.
While AI has underpinned resilience, the investment boom is also adding to inflationary pressures and financial fragility, the IMF said.

"This is a large, front-loaded demand shock" that sees massive investment pouring into sectors such as semiconductors, data centers, and power generation, before any broad productivity gains have materialized, it said in the report.

A potential reassessment of AI-related profitability and productivity prospects could see excessive investment pull back and force a sharp correction in equities. The IMF warned that in a scenario where AI productivity gains fail to materialize, U.S. equities could fall 20% and global growth could end up 1.1% below its baseline estimates by 2028, with Asia 1.7% lower.

Advanced-economy benchmark yields have climbed to multidecade highs as resurgent inflation, the expected path of policy rates and fiscal concerns push up borrowing costs, the IMF said. Technology firms borrowing to finance AI investment are adding to the pressure.

Public debt in advanced economies is projected to reach 115% of GDP by 2031, from 108% in 2025. In emerging and developing economies, it is forecast to climb to 84% from 74%. Primary deficits in the largest economies remain substantially larger than before the pandemic, and governments face higher real interest rates and shorter debt maturities as defense spending pressures mount.
Rebuilding fiscal space is "increasingly urgent," it said, urging governments to keep support for households facing higher energy and food costs "temporary, targeted, and nondistortionary."
Its models put the probability that global inflation exceeds 5% in 2027 at about 35%, up from 30% in April. Risks remain "tilted to the downside," the fund said.
Keri Russell and Matthew Rhys were having their own kind of fun while on the set of The Americans.

During a recent episode of the Dear Chelsea podcast, Russell told host Chelsea Handler that she and Rhys were “having sex all the time,” even while in the characters’ disguises on set. The couple met while filming the FX period spy drama, which ran for six seasons from 2013 to 2018.

“We were falling in love and staying up all night and having sex all the time and just wearing disguises, like, I’m fucking [in] crazy wigs and wearing pearls,” The Diplomat star confessed. “When have you ever worn pearls and [been] fucking in trailers and fucking everywhere. I mean, it was insanity. It was so fun and sneaky, and sexy, and so good.”

The Americans, created by Joseph Weisberg, followed Philip Jennings (Rhys) and Elizabeth Jennings (Russell), two deep-cover KGB spies, who pose as a married American couple running a travel agency in Washington, D.C., during the 1980s Cold War.
After several years of dating, Russell and Rhys welcomed their son Sam in 2016. Russell also shares two children, son River and daughter Willa Lou, with her ex-husband, Shane Deary.

Elsewhere on the podcast, the Felicity actress addressed Rhys not thanking her during his acceptance speeches at the 2026 Emmys for best actor in a comedy series and limited series for his roles in Widow’s Bay and The Beast in Me. Before the ceremony, she recalled telling him, “Take me off your plate. You don’t have to thank me; I know you love me, take me off your plate,” as Rhys was noticeably stressed about the speeches.
Linda Duncombe, a longtime banking executive and independent film producer, died on Sunday. She was 55.

The SAG-AFTRA Foundation, where Duncombe served on the board of directors, announced her death on Monday. She reportedly died of complications from a stroke shortly after being diagnosed with stage 2 lung cancer.

“We are devastated by the sudden loss of our dear friend and fellow Board member, Linda Duncombe,” Courtney B. Vance, president and chair of the SAG-AFTRA Foundation Board, wrote in a statement. “Linda was an extraordinary leader who brought a wealth of experience, influence and relationships to our Board, but what made her truly special was how generously she shared all of it.

“She believed wholeheartedly in the mission of this Foundation and in the importance of supporting the performers who bring stories to life,” Vance continued. “Linda had a remarkable ability to bring people together, open doors and turn her passion for this community into meaningful support for our work. She brought such warmth, wit and enthusiasm to everything she did. She will be deeply missed by our Board and staff, and by the many people whose lives she touched.”

Born on Feb. 10, 1971, in Australia, Duncombe later graduated from Western Sydney University and Harvard Business School. She then spent more than 35 years in banking, including at Citibank in Australia and later at the company’s subsidiary, Citi Fintech, in New York.

Duncombe moved to Los Angeles in 2019 to serve as the chief marketing, data and digital officer at City National Bank. There, she helped establish business, sponsorship and community relations with organizations such as SAG-AFTRA Foundation, the Recording Academy, the Motion Picture Television Fund and Tribeca Film Festival. She also led City National Bank’s efforts to deliver more than $1.8 billion in PPP loans to support the entertainment industry.

In 2022, she joined the SAG-AFTRA Foundation’s board of directors, where she “regularly attended Board meetings and educational programs, engaged with staff and fellow Board members, and drew upon her extensive relationships throughout the entertainment and business communities to raise awareness and critical support for the Foundation’s mission,” according to the organization.

Duncombe also joined the board of directors for EnCorps in 2025, a nonprofit organization founded by Sherry Lansing that focused on connecting STEM professionals with under-resourced public school students. She specifically worked on the EnCorps STEM Teachers Program.
As for her work as a producer, she worked on the films The Queen’s Jewels, Killing Time and Best Pancakes in the County.
Singer-songwriter EJAE was honored at Gyopo’s annual Chuseok Benefit.

The KPop Demon Hunters star is fresh off a whirlwind start to the year after the animated film dominated the awards circuit. EJAE earned herself Golden Globe, Grammy Award and an Oscar along the way. The singer was honored at Gyopo’s 8th annual Chuseok Benefit, which is sponsored by CJ ENM, late last month.

“I’m so honored to be recognized by GYOPO at this year’s Chuseok Benefit. It means so much to be surrounded by a community that celebrates the Korean diaspora and the many different ways we stay connected to our culture, because that connection is at the core of what I do,” she told The Hollywood Reporter.
“It’s been such a special afternoon,” she said. “I’m so proud to celebrate where we come from and what we’re creating together.”

The benefit, held Gyopo board member Ann Soh Woods’ private residence, brought together figures from art, design, entertainment and fashion, including Anicka Yi, Carol Lim,, Dumbfoundead, Jon Moon and fellow Demon Hunters stars Audrey Nuna and Kevin Woo. The event is held in early Autumn during the Korean harvest mon holiday Chuseok, which signifies a time to come together.

“We celebrate EJAE’s exhilarating artistic talent and its power to define an era of popular music and culture. EJAE’s journey to becoming a global music icon is one of perseverance and courage — complex, layered, and full of twists and turns,” Gyopo’s executive director Yoon Ju Ellie Lee said about the honoree.

She added, “Her story has resonated with millions across the globe, but it is the way she shares it, with clarity, honesty, humility and meaningfully contextualized within a diasporic Korean experience, that has touched the hearts of us at Gyopo. EJAE has used her platform to speak openly about her process, pressure, rejection and transformation. In times like these, we savor the opportunity to honor a kindred spirit such as EJAE.”

When he returned to host Saturday Night Live for a third time over the weekend, comedian Shane Gillis garnered a lot of attention for his monologue — and the response has been heated. One of the most vocal critics was Schitt’s Creek star Dan Levy, who posted an Instagram video on Sunday to explain why he took issue with the monologue, and to one part in particular.

The joke in question was when Gillis said, “I haven’t been to the gym in so long, I didn’t know women just dress like whores now? I’m sorry, there’s no other way to describe. Have you seen it? I’ve seen it. The shorts. Have you seen the shorts?”
In his response video, captioned “Ffs,” Levy said in part, “Women wearing short shorts at the gym does not make them whores; it makes the men calling them whores misogynists.”

His comments section was flooded with support, including from a handful of music stars. Jewel thanked Levy, while Wicked star Kristin Chenoweth posted a “100” emoji and Lisa Loeb commented alongside a fire emoji “Thank you.”

Maggie Baird, the activist mother of Billie Eilish and FINNEAS, shared Levy’s video to her Instagram Story with her own lengthy caption. “Thank you [Dan Levy]!” she started. “I literally gasped when [Shane Gillis] said this on [SNL]. I felt it physically (and was reminded of the horrible Bill Burr monologue),” she added, referencing Burr’s controversial 2020 appearance on the sketch comedy show, when he complained that white women had hijacked the “woke” movement and that Pride Month shouldn’t be so long. Baird continued: “I come from the sketch comedy world and am not squeamish around comedy, but how can men and comedy writers still think this is funny! It’s actually dangerous for women to promote this bullsh–.”
Flavor Flav also platformed Levy’s video, sharing an article about his response on X with the message: “Important allyship.”

Maren Morris added to the discourse in her own Instagram post as well, with the message “me being a wh0re at the gym” across a video of herself soundtracked by her song “be a bitch.” In the video, she throws up a middle finger to the camera and finished it off with the caption: “leave my gym short wedgie out of it.”

Gillis hosted Saturday’s show with Rosalía as the musical guest. In addition to it being his third time hosting, Gillis was also briefly a cast member of the show, but he was dismissed soon after the announcement of his casting when previous homophobic and racist jokes of his resurfaced.

Shakira wanted to end her European residency in Madrid on a high note, and for her 13th concert, she surrounded herself with great friends. Maluma, Laura Pausini, Beéle, Dani Martín and Bizarrap joined her for one last night, which also featured dancers from the Carnival of Barranquilla, a drone display and a visibly emotional Shakira bidding farewell.

“There has been a before and after for me. It’s all felt like a dream, and honestly, I don’t want to leave,” the Colombian superstar told the audience. “It’s going to be very, very hard to leave Spain again.”

Announced a week earlier as “The Last Dance,” Monday’s concert (Oct. 12) brought the residency to a total of 13 shows and concluded with four consecutive performances from Oct. 9-12. The finale also coincided with Spain’s National Day (Día de la Hispanidad), with Latin culture strongly present throughout the celebration.

“I’ve prepared so many, many surprises for you tonight,” Shakira teased shortly after starting the show. “Tonight, I’m not holding anything back. I’m going to give you everything, everything, everything I have, because there’s nothing like when a she-wolf meets her pack.”

The first surprise came with Maluma, who returned for the second night in a row to perform “Chantaje” and “Agua” alongside Shakira. “We’ve already done four songs together; we should form a group called Shaluma,” joked Shakira to her compatriot, who replied that he was ready to create many more songs with her.

Later, Shakira paused the show for several minutes to thank the audience and everyone who made possible what she described as one of “the most important” projects of her career. “This residency has been historic for me,” she said, adding that during these weeks, she had also gone through difficult moments, including her father’s health issues and other personal challenges. She said the audience gave her the strength to step on stage every night “with total joy and a full heart… You’ve made me feel like I’m just starting my career, and I will never forget that.”

The superstar then extended her gratitude to everyone who had been part of the show and Macondo Park, as well as Sony Music, Live Nation, her team, musicians and dancers. According to Shakira, more than 10,000 people worked on the production of the show and the themed city that was built around the stadium. She also gave a particularly heartfelt thank-you to her ex Antonio de la Rúa, a current collaborator, introducing him as “a great friend, a soul friend.” Shakira highlighted his support during the tour and his work behind the creation and details of the project.

Following her thank-yous, Laura Pausini took the stage as “the cherry on top,” as Shakira presented her. The Italian artist returned to the residency to perform a duet of “Antología,” as she had during one of the first nights of the residency. Before singing, she took a moment to offer some words, emphasizing what Shakira’s career represents for younger generations of artists. “You are a lesson for so many,” she said. “Just imagine our younger colleagues who see the immense example that you are of a long and very solid career.”

The next guest was Dani Martín, former lead singer of El Canto del Loco and one of the most recognized names in Spanish pop-rock, who joined her for “Te Dejo Madrid.” Shakira introduced him with a nod to the song’s lyrics: “Today, I’m going to sing this with a Madrileño who won’t break my heart.”

Beéle later joined her for a performance of “Algo Tú,” while several Carnival of Barranquilla dancers filled the stage, bringing a piece of her hometown’s celebration to a night that coincided with Spain’s National Day. For “Dai Dai,” the Ghetto Kids joined the celebration in a particularly colorful and vibrant evening.

The final performance also highlighted just how far the residency had come. “When they proposed doing eight concerts here in Madrid, I thought it would be impossible,” Shakira shared. “And look, today is our 13th show. Someone pinch me, please, so I know if this is real or not.” According to the artist, around 700,000 people attended the shows at the Shakira Stadium during the entire residency.

The energy remained high throughout the residency, both on stage and among the audience. Purple wigs and chain belts with coins became a recurring sight among attendees, who embraced some of the most iconic images from different stages of Shakira’s career. Near the end of the show, dozens of drones lit up the sky, first forming the shape of a she-wolf and then a giant “12+1,” the chosen way to mark the final night of the residency.

But one last surprise was still in store. Bizarrap took the stage for the grand finale, stepping behind the turntable to perform “Shakira: Bzrp Music Sessions, Vol. 53” with the singer, keeping the party alive until the final moments of “The Last Dance” and bringing nearly a month of Shakira in Madrid to a spectacular close.
This week, Taylor Swift and The Beatles are meeting up on the Billboard charts in more ways than one.

First, both appear in the top 10 of the Billboard 200 albums chart, with Swift’s The Life of a Showgirl spending its 14th week at No. 1 and The Beatles’ deluxe edition of Rubber Soul arriving at No. 4 following its own stint up top in 1966. In addition, Swift’s latest week at No. 1 on the chart means she and The Beatles are the only acts to ever spend 100 weeks in the Billboard 200 top spot (The Beatles have 132 weeks to Swift’s now-100).

On this week’s Billboard Pop Shop Podcast, Katie & Keith are talking about some of the things these two superstar acts have in common across their respective eras and when Swift might reach (or surpass) some big Beatles landmarks, like their record 20 No. 1 hits on the Billboard Hot 100 songs chart.

Also on the show, we’ve got chart news on how the three acts with the most No. 1s on the Billboard 200 — The Beatles, Swift and Drake — are all in the top 10 together for the very first time. Plus, could Tame Impala and JENNIE’s “Dracula” take a bite out of the No. 1 spot on the Hot 100 soon? And, ADÉLA gets her first Hot 100 top 10 with the viral hit “Nicole Kidman.” And we’re also breaking down the big viral news story of the week: Kelly Clarkson’s heated back-and-forth with a Brooklyn art and magic shop.

The Billboard Pop Shop Podcast is your one-stop shop for all things pop on Billboard‘s weekly charts. You can always count on a lively discussion about the latest pop news, fun chart stats and stories, new music, and guest interviews with music stars and folks from the world of pop. Casual pop fans and chart junkies can hear Billboard‘s executive digital director, West Coast, Katie Atkinson and Billboard’s managing director, charts and data operations, Keith Caulfield every week on the podcast, which can be streamed on Billboard.com or downloaded in Apple Podcasts or your favorite podcast provider.
