Oct. 12 (UPI) -- Federal agents raided Rep. Ilhan Omar's Washington home on Monday as part of an ongoing criminal investigation reportedly involving her immigration to the United States.

Federal agents from Homeland Security Investigations descended upon the home of the Minnesota Democrat early Monday morning, Fox News, ABC News and NBC News reported, citing unnamed sources. The outlets said the investigation into Omar stems from her immigration paperwork.

"Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice," a Justice Department spokesperson said in a statement to ABC News. "This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation."

The Justice Department described the investigation as "criminal" but did not disclose the allegations against Omar, who is running for re-election on Nov. 3, as Democrats seek to win a majority in Congress.
Her office confirmed the raid in a statement, calling it "an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."
"For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back," her office said.

"Now, those attacks have escalated to a pointless federal raid. The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong. No president should be able to use the power of the federal government to intimidate his political enemies."

Omar was born in Mogadishu, Somalia, on Oct. 4, 1982, but fled her native country with her family in 1991 during its civil war to a refugee camp in Kenya. In 1995, she immigrated to the United States and was naturalized as a U.S. citizen at the age of 17 in 2000.

The progressive Democrat was first elected to office in November 2016, winning a seat in the Minnesota House of Representatives, the same year Trump won the presidency, and the two have feuded since. Omar has long been a target of Republican criticism, including insults from Trump, who has called her "garbage" and demanded that she be "sent back from where she came from." Critics have characterized some of his remarks as racist.
In a statement from her personal X account, Omar said she was "ok."
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation," she said.
Democrats lashed out at the Trump administration over the raid, which some framed as a direct attack on U.S. democracy.

Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent from Vermont who caucuses with the Democrats, called Trump "an authoritarian" who wants to "intimidate his political opponents, the media and all those who disagree with him."
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., called the raid "fascism and [an] abuse of office on a scale we have never seen."
"This is the stuff of dictatorships," she said in a statement, vowing to "stand firmly" with Omar.

There is no law categorically prohibiting federal law enforcement from investigating candidates close to an election, but the Justice Department has traditionally avoided overt investigative action during that period because of concerns about influencing elections.

The Trump administration has been investigating claims of fraud in state social service programs in Minnesota. President Donald Trump claims that Somali immigrants have been behind widespread fraud in the state.
According to Rep. Jamie Raskin, reporting indicates that the raid concerned alleged fraud involving immigration paperwork her late father filed decades ago when she immigrated to the United States.

Omar is the latest Democrat and perceived political opponent to the president to face federal investigations. Since returning to the White House, Trump has employed the power of the executive office to impose what critics characterize as punitive measures, against targets ranging from law firms linked his critics to sitting lawmakers, including Rep Jason Crow and Sent. Adam Schiff, as well as former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James.

"In none of these cases has the administration succeeded in doing anything other than wasting taxpayer resources and forcing citizens to waste their own precious time and money defending themselves against bogus charges," Raskin, D-Md., ranking member of the House Committee on the Judiciary, said in a statement.

In defense of the raid, the Republican Party of Minnesota quoted Omar as saying in 2023 that American democracy rests on the rule of law and that it is everyone's responsibility to follow the facts where they lead.
"We couldn't agree more, Congresswoman," the Republican Party of Minnesota said in a statement.
"We're sure you still feel the same way now that it's your front door. Minnesotans will be watching closely, and so will we."
Asked about the raid at the White House, Trump told reporters that what he understands is the investigators were "looking at her very carefuly."
"I've always found her to be totally crooked, personally, but that has nothing to do with me," he told reporters.

"I think she's a terrible person, just a complainer. She comes from a country that is a non-country and then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution. I think she's a terrible person, but that's really up to the DOJ."

Border czar Tom Homan, who took over the Trump administration's immigration enforcement operations in Minnesota earlier this year, said last month in a Fox News appearance that Omar was the subject of a Department of Homeland Security investigation.
Oct. 12 (UPI) -- One person died Monday at Six Flags Over Georgia near Atlanta, police said. Witnesses said the man died in a fall off the Goliath roller coaster.
Cobb County police said several other people were injured in the incident but provided no details Monday.

Aerial video from WXIA-TV of Atlanta showed riders being evacuated from another coaster car that stopped on an incline after the incident. Witnesses told the news outlet that a man was ejected from a car on the ride and hit the ride several times while falling.

"We are deeply saddened by the guest incident at our park today," Six Flags Over Georgia said in a statement. "Our thoughts and heartfelt condolences are with the guest's family, friends and loved ones. We are also providing support to the guests and team members affected.

"The park team and local authorities responded immediately, and we are cooperating fully with local authorities as they complete their investigation. Out of respect for the family's privacy, we will not be sharing additional details at this time," the statement said.

The Goliath roller coaster opened in 2006 and was manufactured by Bolliger & Mabillard. The park's website called it an "intense70-mile-per-hour thrill ride that challenges even the bravest of the brave."
The incident comes a few weeks after Six Flags Magic Mountain in Valencia, Calif., closed its X2 roller coaster permanently after brain injuries and a few deaths were linked to the ride.

"While X2 consistently passed a multitude of safety tests, we have decided to close the ride because we believe it's the right thing to do," park President Brian Oerding said in a statement at the time. "Ride safety is a cornerstone of our business, and when we see guest confidence affected, we take it seriously."

Oct. 12 (UPI) -- A federal judge on Monday blasted the Trump administration after it chopped down at least 430 trees from a public golf course that President Donald Trump has said he wants to overhaul.
"More than just being upset and furious right now, I am just beyond disappointed with the government," U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said during an emergency hearing.

In May, Reyes told administration officials in court that sufficient notice must be provided before they cut down more than 10 trees or did other maintenance on the course in East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C. The judge is overseeing a lawsuit by the DC Protection League and individuals who seek to block an overhaul of the public course, which Trump has said he wants to convert into a professional facility.

The park has three golf courses. Community activists,including those behind the lawsuit, say the government is illegally redeveloping public land per Trump's wishes. The golf course redevelopment could cost between $20 million and $49 million.
Reyes told government officials that they had lost "credibility" with her, as they gave less than a day's notice before cutting down the trees Sunday.
A Justice Department attorney said they'd done their "best" to give notice, but Reyes replied, "No, you did your absolute worst."
"I trusted you all not to do precisely what you have done," thejudge said.
The DC Protection League asked for the emergency temporary restraining order after the trees were cut down Sunday, saying there was "irreplaceable damage" to the course.
Reyes has barred the National Park Service from cutting down any more trees or doing any further work on the course until at least 2 p.m. Tuesday while she decides about a longer block.

The judge said she had no faith that the government wouldn't continue to cut down trees without a court order. "So now we are all going to have a massive fire drill because the government can't be trusted," she said.

Officials did not give any reasons why the hundreds of trees needed to be chopped down so suddenly, Reyes said. She will require that a top Trump appointee at the Department of the Interior testify about the matter Tuesday.
William Shatner wasn’t sure if the audience would approve of his new documentary or not.

When the 95-year-old star took the stage at the Regal Times Square theater for the New York premiere of The Sixty-Year Mission: How Star Trek Changed Television and the World he said “maybe you’ll like it, maybe you won’t.” But, the Captain Kirk actor declared, “you’re going to see a lovely film made by people who cared.”

Focusing on the original Star Trek series, which ran from 1966 to 1969, The Sixty-Year Mission is written and directed by Mark A. Altman, creator of the Inglorious Treksperts podcast. The documentary, which screened during New York Comic Con and hit select theaters this weekend, explores the show’s cultural impact and legacy, and also demonstrates how much it was a product of the political climate of the era in which it was made.

“I think audiences are pleasantly surprised that Sixty-Year Mission shows how the ‘60s shaped Star Trek,” Altman explains. For the film, Altman interviewed dozens of prominent fans and stars, from Shatner and Simon Pegg to Star Trek: The Next Generation stars Jonathan Frakes and Brent Spiner. The president’s niece—and Trek fan—Mary L. Trump praises the show’s pioneering representation, specifically Nichelle Nichols’ Lieutenant Uhura. George Takei, who played Sulu, gives a harrowing account of his time in an internment camp for Japanese Americans during World War II. Others discuss how characters like Spock became heroes for queer fans.

As has been well-documented, these considerations were important for Gene Roddenberry, the show’s creator, who died in 1991. He was a WWII veteran with a progressive bent despite years spent in traditionally conservative spaces like the US Army and the Los Angeles Police Department. Altman insists that “Captain Kirk was ‘JFK: Space Captain,’” and that President Kennedy’s idea of a New Frontier was the final frontier that Trek sought to explore.

Shatner, however, didn’t initially see the show that way at all. “I didn't think in those terms when they offered me the role,” says Shatner, who served as executive producer on Sixty-Year Mission. “I thought, ‘I got a regular paid job.’ Only later did the magic of Star Trek happen.”

Part of that magic, Shatner adds, is how “Star Trek had an effect on people’s lives.” Those people come from many backgrounds, and the show remained accessible because of the very special tension that existed within its politics, Altman explains. “Roddenberry was liberal on social issues but hard-nosed on defense, and that is absolutely what Star Trek is,” he says. “We need our phasers to defeat the Klingons, but we believe in a diverse crew.”

Karim Diané, who plays Jay-Den Kraag on Star Trek: Starfleet Academy, notes that as the person playing the first openly gay Klingon character in the franchise, he’s playing someone who means a lot to viewers. “I wish I could release the DMs because the love I've gotten is overwhelming,” Diané says.

Trek even had a point of view on AI that feels incredibly relevant in 2026 as Trump and Silicon Valley leaders talk about a new era of “superintelligence.” The franchise’s most recognizable AI—the android Data from Next Generation—was an ideal version of the technology. In that series Data consistently struggled to be understood, as both smarter than humans and incapable of emotional intelligence. One episode, “The Measure of a Man,” even addressed whether Data was his own being or merely property.

For Spiner, who played Data, AI’s modern incarnation is far from the thoughtful machine he portrayed. “If only AI could be what Data was: responsible, truly concerned about humanity, considering what serves humans best as opposed to what serves profit best,” he says.

Google’s screenless Fitbit Air made a splash, but it’s been three years since the company updated its display-equipped Charge 6. That older tracker is showing its age, lacking newer automatic workout detection, deeper health metrics, and an IP68 rating. That's where the new Fitbit Edge comes in.

Announced on Monday, it is the successor fitness tracker fans with a screen preference have been waiting for. It sits in a sweet spot at $180—not as costly as a Google Pixel Watch but offering a similar experience in a slimmer, pill-shaped design. And unlike the Pixel Watch, it's compatible with Android and iPhones via the Google Health app. Preorders are available now, and it goes on sale on October 27.

The Edge has a user-replaceable battery, a Fitbit first, aligning with Google’s efforts to make its Pixel Watch more repairable. (Likely also due to new battery regulations set to take effect next year in the European Union.) Repair options will vary by region and availability.

If you find the Pixel Watch’s round face too bulky, the Edge's capsule-shaped alternative might suit smaller wrists better. If the Charge 6’s 1.04-inch display was too small, the Edge upgrades it to a larger 1.34-inch screen. The difference is noticeable, and that extra real estate could make a real impact when glancing at your metrics mid-workout.

The Edge borrows a few more attributes from the Pixel Watch, including an altimeter that uses atmospheric pressure to measure elevation changes. That means it can record elevation gain and loss during outdoor activities, track floors climbed, and add more context to your outdoor stats. It also has a far-field skin temperature sensor, replacing the standard device temperature sensor found in other Fitbits. By bringing some of the Pixel Watch’s more advanced hardware to a fitness-first wearable, Google is giving the Edge a compelling middle-ground position in its lineup at a Fitbit-friendly price.

The Edge inherits the Fitbit Air’s improvements while restoring several Charge 6 features the screenless tracker lacks, including built-in GPS and electrical sensors that work with the electrocardiogram (ECG) app. You can also control music playback on a connected Bluetooth device, as you could with the Charge 6, and Google Maps turn-by-turn directions will arrive later this year.

Google also announced more advanced automatic activity tracking for the Edge, using Gemini Intelligence to identify up to 100 workout types. It can track more than 50 exercise modes, up from 40 on its predecessor. Google will also roll out these features to the Pixel Watch 5 and Air. If they work as promised, it means users won't have to log every activity manually.

With a Google Health Premium subscription, the Edge can track blood pressure trends without manual calibration and insulin resistance trends without requiring a blood draw. Google first announced these capabilities alongside the Pixel Watch 5's debut, but they only became available at the end of September. They’re also available on the Air, keeping Google’s screenless tracker up to date as its lineup expands.

The seven-day battery life remains unchanged, but it’s one of the Edge’s biggest advantages over the Pixel Watch. Like the Air, it takes about 90 minutes to fully charge, which is half an hour less than the Charge 6.

One odd omission is a near-field communication (NFC) sensor, which means the Edge doesn’t support contactless payments through Google Wallet. That’s a downgrade from the Charge 6 and a strange function to lose on a fitness tracker that Google is pitching as a step up from its basic Fitbits.

The Edge introduces new digital and analog clock faces, and the Canyon band color returns from the Pixel Watch 5, alongside five other band styles (Active Band, Active Sport Band, Performance Loop Band, Magnet Band, and Metal Links Band). The Stephen Curry collaboration ($220), which also appeared with the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch 5, is back in the same brown-orange color.

Alongside the Edge, Google is also giving the screenless Fitbit Air a visual upgrade with a new Metal Mesh band. It’s an even dressier strap than the polyurethane Elevated Modern Band. The Air may have initially been designed to disappear on your wrist, but the new band makes it a statement accessory.

If you’re all in on the screenless Fitbit Air, the Edge won’t change your mind. But if you’re not ready to give up a display, the Edge might be a compelling and affordable alternative for both iPhone and Android users. Stay tuned for our review.

Safe in their den, a new litter of cheetah cubs curls up for nap time. One extends an arm and leg in a big stretch, and another stumbles over its siblings to nurse. Five tiny bodies are piled together, one black-spotted coat blending into another.

In a milestone for cheetah conservation, the five cubs were born on October 5 at the Smithsonian’s Conservation Biology Institute in Front Royal, Virginia. When they’re not snoozing, the healthy, young cats are active—they started climbing on their mother on day one.

“Because there’s five of them, somebody’s usually nursing,” Adrienne Crosier, a cheetah biologist and curator of carnivores at the Conservation Biology Institute, tells Smithsonian magazine. “Somebody’s always hungry. Somebody always needs to be groomed. Somebody always needs a bath.”

Zura, who at 5 years old is a first-time mother, has taken it all in stride. She’s an incredibly calm and attentive parent, and she’s dedicating almost every moment of her time to the cubs. Today, she ventured out of the den to get a bite to eat for the first time since their birth.
“That’s very, very normal,” Crosier explains. “But we obviously were happy that she came out, got some food, got some water, and then she went right back to the den with the cubs.”

Born with their eyes closed and ears shut, cheetah cubs are completely dependent on their mothers for survival. It typically takes about four to seven days before they open their eyes, and their ears—initially “flat against their little heads,” Crosier says—will stand up days later.

For now, the care staff is hands-off with the cubs, letting the feline family bond without interference. But they’re keeping a close eye on the cheetah cub cam, which shows scenes from within the den. The online live stream also gives viewers around the world a special window into the animals’ lives, especially since the Front Royal facility is closed to the public.

The cubs will grow rapidly as they nurse. They’ll put on about 50 grams of weight daily—something between a golf ball and an egg. After about three or four weeks, they’ll start to grow curious when Zura leaves the den to eat or drink, gathering at the door when she exits. “They’re going to want to start following her outside,” Crosier says.

Eventually, animal care staff will come into the den and look at the cheetahs to make sure they seem healthy. They’ll pick up a cub, bring it outside to a scale to get its weight, then deposit it back with the family a few minutes later. Staff will mark each baby with a small shave mark in the fur so that they can tell them all apart. At six weeks, they’ll have their first vet exam and vaccinations, and they’ll get transponders implanted for more reliable identification.

Zura herself was born at the institute in 2021, and her mother and grandmother are also at the facility. With the newest litter, that makes four generations of the family in the biologists’ care. The cubs’ 9-year-old father, Flash, also at the institute, has sired seven cubs from previous litters. Cheetah fathers are not involved with raising the youngsters.

Cheetahs are listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, and their global population has plunged by more than 90 percent since 1900. Human activity has fragmented their wild populations, but the cats had been struggling with low genetic diversity since around the end of the last ice age, when an extinction event drove several cheetah species to disappear.

The Conservation Biology Institute breeds cheetahs in accordance with the Cheetah Species Survival Plan, established by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums. Through this initiative, ten facilities across the country select which cheetahs should breed together based on their DNA, temperament, health and other factors. Careful “matchmaking,” which sometimes involves cheetahs traveling hundreds of miles between facilities to meet their possible mate, aims to promote genetic diversity in the population and “produce offspring with the best possible chance of living a healthy life,” per the Smithsonian.
The newborn cubs’ father is considered genetically valuable in this program, so the little cheetahs will likely have a big role to play in the future of their species.
With these cubs, the Conservation Biology Institute has now reached 90 cheetah births at the facility, representing 21 litters.

“Every litter is so important,” Crosier says. “Every cheetah that’s born is an ambassador for its species and … can contribute in the future, potentially, to help with the conservation of the animals in the wild.”

A new-age swamp is bubbling up inside the lobby of New York City’s Museum of Modern Art (MoMA). Beginning next week, visitors will find themselves stepping through a colorful, pulsing digital ecosystem that may seem a world away from the city’s urbanity and frenetic pace.

“Wetland,” an immersive exhibition by the Danish artist Jakob Kudsk Steensen, thrives in this sensory disconnect. Opening on October 12, MoMA’s newest show is a futuristic, digital vision of nature. It also opens a portal back to the mucky landscapes that major cities—including New York—were founded upon.
The installation harnesses macro photogrammetry and game-engine software (the architecture behind video games) to simulate the movements, sounds and sights of a large-scale swamp.

Wall-spanning screens display photographs and 3D scans of real-life wetlands. Digitally altered field recordings of amphibians and susurrating riverine rhythms have been mixed with human vocals, including those from the Venezuelan musician Arca.
“At MoMA, it’s made to envelop you—but with a sense of … dance,” Kudsk Steensen tells the New York Times’ Frank Rose. “Things appear. They vanish. They’re dark. They’re bright. They’re vocal.”
“Wetland” features just a single work of art: the simulated swamp installation known as Berl-Berl, which Kudsk Steensen has allowed to evolve since its creation in 2021.

Both Berl-Berl’s form and name were inspired by the swamps surrounding Berlin, many of which have fallen victim to urban development. The artist collaborated with Berlin’s natural history museum to devote months to studying the landscape. A combination of photography, sound recording, kayaking, swamp-slogging and archival research left Kudsk Steensen with a trove of material documenting humanity’s relationship with wetland habitats. The result was Berl-Berl, first installed in Berghain, a nightclub located in a sprawling decommissioned East German power plant.

“In the beginning, I thought I was just making an immersive show, with some nature sounds, some screens and some things that are moving around,” Kudsk Steensen told Dazed’s Juule Kay in 2021, ahead of Berl-Berl’s debut. “But when I walked around in the space, I started to whistle and clap and noticed the echo.”

Each iteration of the installation—in Denmark, South Korea, Switzerland and elsewhere in Berlin—remains in a state of flux. At times, folklore plays a central role. Triglav, a three-headed god from Slavic folklore, makes an appearance at MoMA in the form of a giant tree. Although absent from the MoMA iteration, the shape-shifting water spirit Nøkken, who is said to appear to travelers as a handsome, music-playing young man, often appears in the digital swamp, too.

“We used to sing to the world in order to navigate it,” Kudsk Steensen said in 2024. “And in Europe, in the past, there were many practices to create songs as ways of mapping terrains, especially rivers and swamps, because these are ever-changing landscapes.”
- In July, the United Nations added the Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge, which protects a swamp sprawled between Florida and Georgia, to its list of UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
- UNESCO described it as a “diverse mosaic of wetlands, savannas and forests” with stunning biodiversity.

In “Wetland,” Kudsk Steensen uses macro photogrammetry—the practice of turning microscopic details into larger images—to illuminate and archive the overlooked textures of wetland soils, plants and currents. Cutting-edge tools help bring the artist closer to nature instead of dividing him from it. “Technology for me, in the sense of being a medium, is a connector,” the artist has said.

“It’s fascinating,” Paola Antonelli, MoMA’s senior curator of architecture and design, tells the Times. “This most technological part of the museum is the one that really digs into nature, into consciousness.”
“Wetland” will be on view at the Museum of Modern Art in New York City from October 12, 2026, to March 7, 2027.
Navanethem Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.”

The Nobel committee lauded the 85-year-old South African jurist and former United Nations human rights chief for her “commitment to universal legal principles” and her “firm moral compass” throughout her long career.

Through decades of work in South African and international courts, Pillay, who is known as Navi, has helped shape legal efforts to hold governments and individuals accountable for human rights abuses and mass atrocities.

Pillay was born in Durban, South Africa, in 1941. She grew up in a poor family of Indian Tamil descent. The daughter of a bus driver, she pursued a career in law at a time when discrimination limited opportunities for non-white South Africans. She established her own law firm in 1967 and in 1988 became the first South African at Harvard Law School to become a Doctor of Juridical Science, the school’s most advanced degree.

Under apartheid, Pillay and other non-white South Africans were “treated like dirt,” she told the Agence France-Presse (AFP) in 2023. But rather than letting the mistreatment keep her down, she opted to “fight every step of the way.”
“I always had a sense of confidence about who I am and how you confront any kind of discrimination,” she told AFP. “Open your mouth and speak up, condemning it.”

Pillay’s early career centered on defending anti-apartheid activists, including Nelson Mandela, whom she joins as a Nobel Peace Prize laureate. In 1995, she broke another barrier when she became the first non-white woman appointed to South Africa’s High Court.

Her work subsequently took her onto the international stage. In 1999, Pillay became a judge and president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, which investigated crimes committed during the 1994 genocide. During her tenure, she helped establish important legal precedents recognizing sexual violence as potential acts of genocide and crimes against humanity, bringing international attention to the estimated 100,000 to 250,000 Rwandan women who were raped during the three-month massacre.
“Rape had always been regarded as one of the spoils of war,” she said at the time. “Now it is a war crime, no longer a trophy of war.”

From 2008 to 2014, Pillay served as the U.N. high commissioner for human rights. From 2021 to 2025, she chaired the U.N. Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, leading an investigation that concluded Israel committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip. (Israel strongly rejected the report.)

Pillay also served as a judge on the International Criminal Court and currently serves as an ad hoc judge on the International Court of Justice, the U.N.’s primary judicial body, in an ongoing case assessing whether Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.

By honoring Pillay, the Nobel committee sought to remind the world that international law is the “foundation for a more peaceful world,” Jørgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Nobel committee, said during the award announcement.
“International law has never been perfect,” Frydnes added. But it “sets the standards. Legal measures do prevent acts of war and violence. That is a fact.”

Pillay learned that she had won the prize while attending an international law conference in Courtroom 600 of the Nuremberg Palace of Justice, where top Nazi leaders were indicted and tried for their crimes during World War II.
“At this venue, your applause means a great deal,” she said after hearing the news. “But being a lawyer and a judge, I still want to verify this information.”
Pillay is the first South African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize. Four South African men—Albert Lutuli, Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela and F.W. de Klerk—have received the award.

Swedish inventor Alfred Nobel established the Nobel Peace Prize, as well as prizes for physiology or medicine, chemistry, literature and physics, with a bequest in his will, which he drafted in 1895. The prizes were first awarded in 1901. The economics prize was established in Nobel’s memory in 1968.

This year, the Nobel Peace Prize celebrates its 125th anniversary, with 287 individuals and organizations nominated for the award. The committee noted that the 2026 prize “springs directly” from Nobel’s will, which stated that the award should be given to those who have “conferred the greatest benefit to humankind.”

Pillay is “one of the great defenders of international legal principles in our time,” according to the committee. “[Her] commitment to justice and human dignity is a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.”
Where it is from: Baffin Island, Nunavut, Canada

This wooden figurine was discovered in 1977 in an early house built by the ancestors of the Inuit on Baffin Island in northern Canada. The unique carving represents a person wearing European clothing and a cross on their chest. Dated to 1350, the figurine is the earliest Indigenous representation of a European anywhere in the Western Hemisphere and probably depicts a Norseman.

The tiny driftwood carving, which is currently on display at the Canadian Museum of History, measures just 2.1 inches (5.4 centimeters) tall. According to the museum, the featureless face and stumpy arms are common in 14th-century Inuit carvings, but the depiction of a non-Inuit is unique.

The mysterious figure wears a long robe or tunic with a cross on the front — a garment that is similar to those worn in the 11th to 13th centuries by Norse Christians from Greenland. The Norse sagas mention a place called "Helluland," which Leif Eriksson (also spelled Erikson) visited in the early 11th century and is most likely Baffin Island.

Around A.D. 1000, Norse explorers landed in what is now Newfoundland and set up camp at a site archaeologists call l'Anse aux Meadows. Wood buildings and remains from iron production are all that is left of the earliest European settlement in the Americas.

The Norse likely made multiple trips from Greenland to Canada over the centuries in order to trade metal and cloth with the Inuit's ancestors, known as the Thule, and procure walrus ivory in return, as European-origin artifacts have been found in early Inuit houses on Baffin Island. But the Norse eventually abandoned their westward trade routes, possibly due to the resistance of the Indigenous people and the long distance.

This wooden figurine may commemorate a meeting between the Inuit and the Norse and is especially important because it was crafted long before sustained contact in the late 15th century, according to the museum. It is also the earliest evidence of the Indigenous perspective of visitors from the east, revealing which characteristics of the Norse the artisan observed and felt were important to depict.

In the latest episode of Counter Culture, Pat Burrow, technical director at International Lubricants, discusses the causes of torque converter shudder. He also explains the importance of transmission fluid and how friction modifiers can help technicians diagnose and address the problem.
Burrow Explains Causes of Torque Converter Shudder

Burrow explains that torque converter shudder often feels like driving over railroad tracks, with vibrations ranging from barely noticeable to severe. Although mechanical wear, solenoids and transmission programming can contribute, depleted fluid additives frequently play a significant role.
“Transmission fluid is probably the most complicated lubricant you have in your vehicle,” Burrow said.
Beyond lubrication, transmission fluid provides cooling, wear protection, hydraulic operation and smooth clutch engagement.

Burrow explains that modern automatic transmission fluids contain friction modifiers designed for specific applications. However, demanding driving conditions can accelerate additive depletion, sometimes causing shudder after just 20,000 to 30,000 miles.

Burrow emphasizes asking customers about vehicle mileage, driving conditions and specific applications before recommending a solution. Heavy loads, high temperatures and stop-and-go traffic can increase the likelihood of fluid-related problems.

Burrow also discusses how friction modifiers can serve as diagnostic tools. If a friction modifier reduces or eliminates shudder, technicians can identify fluid-related issues before pursuing mechanical repairs.
“If the shutter went away, boom, they knew instantly what the problem was. It was fluid,” Burrow said.
However, Burrow cautions that worn solenoids, valve bodies and other mechanical problems may require repairs that fluid additives cannot address.

Schaeffler and Qorix have entered into a strategic partnership to jointly develop, integrate and market software-based platform solutions. The companies will focus on future vehicle architectures and intelligent machines. Together, the companies aim to advance integrated hardware and software solutions for central vehicle computers and software-defined architectures.

The collaboration combines Schaeffler’s expertise in system integration and safety-critical driving and comfort functions with Qorix’s production-ready middleware technologies. It also incorporates Qorix’s integration expertise in central computing platforms and active involvement in the Eclipse S-CORE open-source ecosystem.

“With our platform and integration expertise, Schaeffler is laying the foundation for central software-defined vehicle architectures. Qorix complements this foundation with production-ready middleware and a strong open-source approach, enabling us to bring scalable solutions to market faster and more efficiently,” said Thomas Stierle, CEO E-Mobility at Schaeffler AG.
Schaeffler, Qorix Address New Vehicle Architecture Requirements

The shift from distributed electronic control unit architectures to central high-performance computing platforms presents the automotive industry with new requirements. The industry needs reliable middleware and software platforms that meet standards for scalability, security and production readiness.
Schaeffler contributes hardware platforms, cross-domain controller solutions and many years of experience in system integration.

Qorix complements these strengths with Qorix Performance, which provides deterministic communication and end-to-end management throughout the entire product life cycle. The technology also supports functional safety in accordance with ISO 26262.
Together, the partners aim to reduce integration efforts, shorten development times and accelerate the industrialization of software-defined vehicle architectures.
Open Source Provides Technological Foundation
Both companies participate in Eclipse S-CORE, an open-source software framework for software-defined vehicles.
Their involvement supports faster, more consistent development and reduces integration efforts. It also enables software reuse across vehicle generations and customer programs.

“With Schaeffler as a strategic partner, we are accelerating exactly what drives us: bringing production-ready, open-source-based software platforms to market faster. Qorix Performance combined with Schaeffler’s system integration and compute expertise creates a compelling offering for automotive manufacturers and Tier 1 suppliers that want to actively shape the transition to software-defined architectures,” said Markus Schupfner, CEO of Qorix.

Ever drive a vehicle that just doesn’t feel right anymore? Maybe it wanders down the highway. Maybe there’s a clunk every time you hit a pothole. Maybe the steering wheel isn’t centered, the tires are wearing unevenly, or it just doesn’t inspire the confidence it used to.

The truth is, steering and suspension problems rarely come from a single worn out part. Every control arm, ball joint, tie rod, sway bar link, and bushing work together as one connected system. Super Cruise is GM’s hands-free driver-assistance system, offered on certain 2019-205 GM vehicles. Feature-wise, it combines adaptive cruise control, automatic braking, lane centering, driver monitoring, GPS and high-definition map data.

In the shop, diagnosis starts by separating a component fault or configuration problem from a normal system inhibit. A missing condition or failure in any of the above-mentioned areas can prevent engagement.

On an approved mapped road, Super Cruise uses Adaptive Cruise Control to manage speed and following distance while the lane-control system commands electric power steering to center the vehicle. The forward camera supplies lane information, and Adaptive Cruise Control sensing hardware tracks traffic ahead. The engine and electronic brake control modules carry out acceleration and braking requests. Because these modules exchange network data, a voltage, communication or configuration fault outside the camera can disable the system.

Super Cruise also compares GPS position with its map database. GM service information identifies the K179 Automated Driving Mapping Module and a LiDAR-scanned map database. Map and GPS-enhancement updates are downloaded through the vehicle’s OnStar Wi-Fi connection. The K73 telematics module supplies GPS and connectivity functions. If the vehicle cannot establish its location or does not have usable road data, Super Cruise cannot confirm that the road is eligible.

Before condemning hardware, verify the enabling conditions. Adaptive Cruise Control must be on, the Forward Collision System set to Alert and Brake, the road approved in the map database, lane markings visible, sensors unobstructed and the driver attentive. Teen Driver mode cannot be active. An OnStar plan and accepted terms may also be required. Requirements vary by model year and RPO, so identify the vehicle configuration before testing.

The secondary DIC message is often more useful than the general statement that Super Cruise is unavailable. “No Road Information” may indicate an ineligible road, an interchange, reconstruction, missing map data or lost GPS. The message “Sensors Can’t Find Lane Lines” can result from weak markings, glare or precipitation. “Sensor Blocked” points toward contamination. Other normal inhibits include an exit lane, a sharp curve, failure to center the vehicle or excessive speed. The referenced GM application lists 85 MPH, although limits are calibration-dependent.

“Could Not Recognize Face,” “Can’t See Face Clearly,” “Driver Attention Assist Unavailable,” momentary engagement followed by a takeover warning, and unexplained disengagement can originate in the monitoring system. Check for glare, a dirty lens, obstructions, steering-column position, a hand covering the infrared emitters, a loose B292 camera in the upper shroud, wiring damage or failed emitters. These complaints may occur without a DTC.

First, record the exact messages the customer received, along with road and location, weather, lighting, speed, engagement time and repeatability. Ask them about recent windshield, collision, steering, alignment, suspension, camera, radar or module work. Verify the OnStar account and terms when applicable, plus Wi-Fi and map-update status.

Next, perform GM’s vehicle diagnostic system check. Confirm battery state of charge, 9-16 V operating voltage where specified, clean and tight cables and grounds, intact fuses, seated connectors, correct power modes and the absence of interfering aftermarket equipment. Inspect lenses, radar areas and the steering-column camera before connecting the scan tool.

Run a full vehicle DTC scan and document every non-communicating module, DTC, symptom byte and current or history status. Do not erase evidence first. Diagnose voltage, internal-module, communication, power-mode and serial-data authentication faults before the Super Cruise symptom. Check applicable bulletins and calibrations. On covered 2021-2024 vehicles, intermittent startup U1624 in K124 may be a false loss-of-Ethernet fault caused by K73 telematics software; follow the bulletin and update K73. For other programmable modules, GM directs current software and a retest before replacement. Cruise data can retain the last eight disengagement reasons and the most recent engagement inhibit.

For “No Road Information” without a related DTC, move the vehicle to an open-sky area and inspect the K73 telematics data, including Number of Satellites Tracked when available. A value that remains at zero, or an incorrect location during an OnStar blue-button check, supports a GPS or telematics fault on vehicles covered by the applicable bulletin. Separate that failure from temporary map, road or reception limits.

For low-light face-recognition complaints, verify all three infrared emitters on each side of the steering-wheel light bar. GDS2 can command them through K124 Image Processing Module 1 Processor 2 under Configuration Reset Functions and Driver Monitoring System Illumination Command. GM recommends a phone camera with a long-exposure function because infrared output may be difficult to see. If one side is dark, follow the VIN-specific circuit diagnostics.

Programming, setup and calibration requirements differ across the 2019-2025 range. Confirm RPO content and follow the exact SI procedure after related components are replaced or disturbed. Some 2022-2023 vehicles with RPO 07Z use an image-processing module only to complete CAN circuits. Installing a functional replacement can create a “Take Steering Wheel” message unless the published configuration procedure is followed.

Complete all required programming, setup and calibrations, then clear the codes only as directed. Road-test the vehicle safely on a known compatible route and reproduce the original conditions. Confirm that the enabling indicators appear, the original DIC message does not return, driver monitoring responds and no faults reset. A successful bay check does not prove the complaint is resolved by itself.

Wheel balancers and tire changers from the Ranger Division of BendPak have earned ETL certification, the company announced. All current models meet applicable UL and CSA safety standards in the United States and Canada.

Intertek Testing Services independently tested the equipment and validated its compliance with electrical, pneumatic and mechanical safety requirements. Intertek is a nationally recognized testing laboratory.
BendPak Completes 18-Month Certification Project
The certification followed an 18-month BendPak project to overhaul critical internal components and safety systems. The company redesigned the equipment to meet applicable standards.
The project included upgrades to electrical architecture, structural components and mechanical and pneumatic systems.
The company redesigned or replaced components that did not meet the required criteria. BendPak also reconfigured systems and incorporated additional safeguards.
BendPak says it then subjected every modification to testing before the equipment could achieve certification.
The ETL mark on the product label identifies certified equipment.
Certification Covers Ranger Wheel Service Equipment
Certified Ranger wheel service equipment includes:
- LS45DS Laser-Spot sonar wheel balancer
- RB30T heavy-duty truck and passenger car wheel balancer
- R76ATR single-tower tilt-back tire changer
- R980DP dual-assist swing-arm tire changer
- R80EX dual-tower tilt-back tire changer

One of the most recognized names in American motorcycle performance is joining the inaugural Builders Cup at AIMExpo 2027. S&S Cycle will award a brand-new engine to the winning builder when selected custom motorcycles compete in The Builders Cup fueled by Drag Specialties, March 3–5 in Orlando, Florida.

Founded in 1958, S&S Cycle has maintained close connections with builders, racers, tuners and innovators in motorcycle performance. As a result, its involvement adds industry credibility to a competition celebrating the creativity and influence of today’s custom builders.
S&S Cycle Engine Joins Builders Cup Prize

During AIMExpo, selected builders will showcase their motorcycles inside The Builders Club. There, custom motorcycle culture will connect with manufacturers, distributors, dealers, media and other powersports leaders attending AIMExpo.
The Builders Cup winner will leave Orlando with bragging rights and a brand-new S&S Cycle engine.

“Builders have been part of the S&S Cycle story from the beginning,” said Howard Kelly, vice president of marketing at S&S Cycle. “They are the people willing to experiment, challenge convention and find new ways to turn performance into something personal and The Builders Cup celebrates exactly that kind of creativity. Putting an S&S engine in the hands of the winner gives us an opportunity to recognize a great build, while helping fuel whatever they create next.”

“A great custom motorcycle makes you stop and look, but the best builds stay with you long after and that’s what The Builders Cup is all about,” said Andre Albert, director of market expansion and events for the Motorcycle Industry Council. “Having S&S Cycle provide an engine for the winner speaks volumes about the caliber of this competition and the builders behind it. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) plans to modernize its outdated vehicle lighting standards, saying doing so will make America’s roads safer for all drivers, according to a press release.

NHTSA says an update to Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standard No. 108 is “long overdue,” and that it will accelerate the rulemaking process by consulting with industry stakeholders, safety advocates, and technical experts.
The release states the discussions will cover key safety and engineering challenges, including:
- “Addressing headlight glare: Examining the role that modern headlighting technology has on glare for other road users and making appropriate changes.
- “Modernizing lighting technology: Improving rules for LEDs, dusk sensors, automatic high beams, and replaceable light sources.
- “Improving performance: Evaluating how headlamp height and aim affect driver visibility.
- “Updating testing and materials: Streamlining test procedures for plastic optics and replaceable lenses.
- “Aligning global standards: Harmonizing U.S. vehicle lighting regulations with international safety standards.”
The release notes that this is the first time in more than 25 years that NHTSA is using negotiated rulemaking to update its vehicle lighting standards.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy plans to appoint up to 18 stakeholders across vehicle lighting manufacturers, motor vehicle equipment associations, safety organizations, research institutions, and engineering associations.
According to NHTSA’s rulemaking notice, it proposes the following representation:
- “Four representatives from vehicle lighting manufacturers or lighting retailers;
- “Two representatives from national motor vehicle manufacturers;
- “Four representatives from national motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment manufacturing associations;
- “Two representatives from national motor vehicle or motor vehicle equipment safety organizations;
- “Three representatives from educational institutions or research institutions, or testing organizations within the United States; and
- “Three representatives from national professional engineering associations or standard-setting associations.”
The notice states that the committee will be “tasked with developing a detailed term sheet consisting of consensus recommendations to inform the agency’s rulemaking proposal.”
“NHTSA has long recognized the complexity of FMVSS No. 108 and the need to modernize the standard to facilitate new vehicle designs and emerging technologies,” the notice states.

It notes that NHTSA initiated rulemaking action RIN 2127-AL95 in the Spring 2018 Unified Agenda of Regulatory and Deregulatory Actions. The notice states that the ongoing effort led to a rulemaking petition from Osram Sylvania regarding LED replacement light sources.

“Given the technical challenges of updating these legacy requirements, NHTSA recognizes that the expertise of outside stakeholders is essential in any highly technical discussion of revising FMVSS No. 108,” the notice states.

“The effort will cover various topics of modernization, such as glare caused by headlighting systems, replaceable light sources, dusk sensors, plastic optical materials, semiautomatic beam switching, minimum lamp size requirements, lower beam photometry, upper beam photometry, on-vehicle headlamps performance that considers aim and mounting height, auxiliary lamp requirements, three-wheel motorcycle installation requirements, obsolete physical test requirements for associated equipment, physical test procedures for lamps that use replaceable lenses, and harmonization to international standards.”
NHTSA says an abstract published in the Unified Agenda for RIN 2127-AL95 includes some of the topics.

“Today’s standards do not allow automakers to deploy the latest safety-improving lighting technologies, so we are bringing key experts and stakeholders together to modernize our standards and address potential causes of glare,” said NHTSA Administrator Jonathan Morrison in the release. “This collaborative approach will allow us to update outdated regulations, foster innovation, and keep everyone on our roads safer.”

NHTSA has asked for public comments on the rulemaking scope and committee membership. It also requests formal membership nominations. The deadline for comments and membership applications is Nov. 9. Both can be submitted here under Docket No. NHTSA-2026-1981.
In 2022, NHTSA issued a final rule allowing OEMs to install adaptive driving beam (ADB) headlights on new vehicles to increase visibility and reduce headlight glare.

NHTSA ruled that ADBs would improve safety for pedestrians and bicyclists by making them more visible at night and would help prevent crashes by better illuminating animals and objects in and along the road, according to the final rule. However, NHTSA states in the rule that “glare dosage,” or the amount of glare, “has not established, and does not know of, a quantified relationship between glare dosage and crash risk.”

Toyota has opened a new battery center in Saline, Michigan, calling it “the next chapter of its electrification transformation.”

According to a press release from the automaker, the Toyota Battery Center of North America (TBC) gives Toyota Michigan-based battery teams increased capabilities to evaluate and develop technology across the full battery-development cycle, from sourcing raw materials and customer applications to recycling.

“Toyota has long been at the forefront of battery development,” said Keita Moritsu, Toyota Motor North America R&D senior vice president and chief technology officer, in the release. “This center is where that leadership expands to North America — and where we’re building its next chapter.”
On site, teams of engineers and technicians assess battery performance and develop new technologies for use in hybrid, plug-in hybrid, hydrogen, and fully electric vehicles.

Toyota says the 30,000-square-foot facility serves as a central hub for development and evaluation, in partnership with Toyota’s North American manufacturing network, to support battery evaluation for Toyota Battery Manufacturing North Carolina, as well as the OEM’s vehicle manufacturing plants across North America.

“For Toyota customers, this facility means Toyota engineers can detect and resolve field concerns faster and closer to the source,” said Jordan Choby, Group Vice President of Powertrain, in the release. “It also means we can develop longer-lasting batteries designed to perform in the conditions American drivers face every day.”

Toyota says it will share research access at the facility with the University of Michigan Electric Vehicle Center. As a founding member of the center, Toyota says the program is a part of its commitment to developing the next generation of battery engineers and technicians in Michigan.

In 2025, Toyota began production at Toyota Battery Manufacturing North Carolina, its first battery plant opened outside of Japan. Located in Liberty, the $14 billion facility houses lithium-ion battery production lines for hybrid electric, plug-in hybrid electric, and battery electric vehicles.

Through a joint venture with two other companies, Honda has developed underlaying technology for a magnetic-coupling wireless power transfer road system (WPT road system), which will enable wireless in-motion charging of EVs, according to a press release.
Honda R&D, Taisei Corp. (Taisei), and Taisei Rotec Corp. (Taisei Rotec) plan to conduct demonstration testing of the system beginning in the Japanese 2027 fiscal year.
The system combines proprietary technology from each of the companies:
- Honda: High-power-density power receiver/transmitter units compatible with DC power distribution
- Taisei: High-response DC power supply system
- Taisei Rotec: Technology for embedding equipment in roads

“With these technologies, the system achieves high-power wireless power transfer (WPT) and excellent ease of installation in road pavement, envisioning applications for a wide range of mobility products, from passenger EVs to large commercial EVs,” the release states.

Honda says it has been working on dynamic wireless power transfer (DWPT) technology since 2021. The technology supplies power to vehicles while they are in motion and reduces the frequency of charging needed at home or at a charging station, the release states.

“Initially, Honda will strive to put DWPT technology into practical use in the logistics and transportation sectors, where DWPT technology is expected to deliver significant benefits,” the release states.

Honda, Taisei, and Taisei Rotec have been conducting research and development of the magnetic-coupling WPT road system since 2025, according to the release. This has resulted in the development of the underlaying technology for the system.

This includes conducting experiments and validation testing on a test roadway at the Future Technology Field for Taisei Group/Satte (T-FIELD/SATTE). The tests verified the effectiveness of the technologies for a WPT system, road pavement structures, and road construction methods intended for demonstration testing on public roads with large commercial vehicles, according to the release.
- DC distribution-based ground assembly (GA) systems that connect multiple GA units embedded in the road using a DC connection
- A vehicle assembly (VA) unit installed on the vehicle

Honda says that to achieve the real-world implementation of a WPT road system, it is essential to develop GA units and pavement structures with sufficient strength to withstand the loads of large commercial vehicles and a power transfer system capable of handling high-power transfer to EVs driving at high speeds, while also offering excellent practicality for installation in roads.
Testing at the T-FIELD/SATTE focused on GA units and pavement structures capable of withstanding the traffic of large vehicles with a gross vehicle weight of about 20 tons.
It also tested whether the DC power supply systems can supply high-power electricity to a DC distribution-based GA system with high responsiveness and stability.
The GA units were also tested for highly practical installation and future upgrades.

Next, the companies plan to begin testing long-term durability in late 2026 through a loading test equivalent to 1 million wheel loads using actual vehicles. It will also conduct DWPT performance tests and evaluate measures to address electromagnetic field leakage.
“Through these tests, the three companies will strive to ensure both power transfer performance and the safety of the GA units as structures embedded in the roadway,” the release states.

After this phase, the companies plan to further verify performance at high power output levels of up to 150 kW for potential application to large commercial vehicles, as well as verification of the reliability of WPT performance for vehicles traveling at high speeds.

Honda says that all three companies will participate in the “Tateyama Project” starting during the Japanese 2027 fiscal year. It will include demonstration testing of DWPT technology conducted by East Nippon Expressway Company Limited on the Tateyama Expressway in Chiba, Japan.

“Striving to realize a sustainable mobility society where people can enjoy freedom of mobility well into the future, Honda will continue to pursue co-creation with a diverse range of partners beyond the automotive industry, including road infrastructure-related businesses, government agencies and energy-related businesses,” the release states.

Gunshots erupted from solid ground towards a boat that ferried Panamanian soldier Albis Fajardo and his team during a counter-drug mission along the country’s Pacific coastline.

The team attempted to return fire as they pulled back from a harrowing effort to target a cartel leader. Fajardo, then early into his military career, felt his adrenaline surge as he realized the team had been unsuccessful: A bullet had torn through the flesh of his friend.

Over a decade later, with the early autumn sun sinking over Panamanian base Aeronaval Cristóbal Colón, the 47-year-old, now a first sergeant, recounted the ordeal. His friend survived, but the horror changed Fajardo’s life.
The brush with death, he said, fueled him to learn as much as he could, militarily, and eventually led him to become an instructor at the U.S. Army’s Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama.

The class, offered for decades in the Central American nation before it was shuttered in 1999, has resumed in partnership between U.S. and Panamanian forces, with Panamanian service members teaching and attending the 18-day course.
As Panama’s troops have trained, lived — and in some cases, fought — in such environments, they are largely seen by U.S. personnel as the ultimate masters of the terrain.

Lt. Col. Andrew Eagen, who heads the U.S. Jungle Operations Training Center in Panama, said that as U.S. forces developed the course, they became quickly attuned to the deft tactics their Panamanian counterparts had developed for survival.
“They are the experts of this environment. We will never catch up,” he told Military Times in a mosquito-riddled interview at the jungle school.

“This does not exist in the continental United States,” he said, gesturing to the lush canopy, which was twinkling with the day’s last glimmers of sun and abuzz with the evening hum of jungle creatures. “We do not have an exposure to it. They do, and they have incredible techniques and an incredible level of comfort that the average American [does not].”
Fajardo is one of nine Panamanian instructors — from three branches of the country’s armed forces — who teach at the reestablished school.
The instructors assist in some parts of the course, but lead in areas where students learn about jungle survival, Eagen said.
In addition to the leading group, more than 10 Panamanian service members attended the course in which Military Times took part, according to Eagen.
Throughout each exercise, Panamanian troops sat interspersed with U.S. personnel and were placed in squads with a Spanish-speaking U.S. participant for course assignments.
Though the language barrier admittedly made some tactical movements difficult, U.S. personnel seemingly learned just from observing their Panamanian counterparts.

During one practical exercise, one squad had to hide in the jungle, cover their tracks to erase any disturbance to the foliage, and position themselves so they would be alerted to any incoming intruders.
The other squad’s job was to hunt down the hiding squad using tracking clues, the activity forming a tense game of tactical hide-and-seek.
The hunters ultimately won, thanks to one Panamanian squadmate who spotted a tiny vine that appeared slightly too parallel to the ground.

One rule of the jungle? Nothing is a straight line. The Panamanian student correctly identified the trailing plant, hovering inches above the muddy ground, as a hasty trip wire. Made using a vine and a piece of trash, it would have alerted the hiding squad to the hunters’ presence.

When the two groups gathered to discuss the interaction, the lanewalker found that the Panamanian student in the other squad had set up the tripwire; a particularly impressive development, considering a tripwire class was scheduled for later in the day.
During that class, an American instructor showed students how to create different forms of tripwires that could act as early warning systems. Some set off rattling cans. Others used fauna.

Before letting students practice, the instructor shared stories from Panamanian cadres who once operated in the Darién Gap, a roadless land bridge of brutally dense, remote jungle that spans 60-plus miles between Panama and Colombia and has been notoriously rife with human and drug trafficking.
Trip wires there are not historical relics of warfare from decades ago, the instructor said. Cartel members are using them now.
Several instructors, including Fajardo, have attended Panama’s own jungle school, called Panajungla.
Fajardo shook his head and shivered as he recounted the intense course in which participants were forced to survive on their own in the Teribe region of Panama’s Bocas del Toro province.
Students of the Panamanian course must shop at the “supermarket de la selva” — the jungle supermarket — to eat, using machetes to prepare or kill any nourishment they can find, Fajardo said.
Fajardo’s prized jungle delicacy is ñame, a tropical root vegetable similar to a yam. He also appreciates the taste of grubs, he said, which he likens to butter.
Tucked neatly into each Panamanian instructor’s backpack, razor-sharp machetes sat nestled in intricately carved leather coverings.

The U.S. Army teaches machete training in its jungle school, but some Panamanian instructors have attended a separate, more intensive course on using the long, daunting blade. It can clear brush, help prepare food, carve shelter and even help start a fire.
To Fajardo, it is the single most important tool for survival in the jungle. And with a smile, he jokingly referred to the machete as “mi esposa,” or my wife, in English.
To date, the U.S. Army is developing the course to dedicate at least 20 of its 120 spots to partner forces and at least 15 to Panamanians.
Though no other countries have sent soldiers yet, Eagen is confident that the school is close to having Colombian students join.

The U.S. has partnered with Colombia’s Lancero course, which is similar to Ranger School, and all three countries exchange information. Panama supports hosting Colombian forces, Eagen added, as “they have a direct relationship with the country.
“They have a lot of shared bilat right there at the Darién,” Eagen said, “so both Panamanian leaders and Colombian leaders want them to be first.”
Panama’s expertise in navigating such unforgiving terrain, meanwhile, has also prompted other countries, like Costa Rica and Brazil, to express interest in the course, Eagen said.

Other jungle courses worldwide have so far informed the new U.S. Army jungle school’s curriculum, and Eagen said the Army is designing a scenario construct for the school using threat characteristics seen by Panamanian service members.

And while Panamanian forces often confront small-team drug trafficking operations attempting to establish supply lines, Eagen was clear that the Army endeavored to replicate a potential combat environment, not the country’s security situation.

“That is not the premise of us being in Panama,” he said. “We try to make sure there are clear boundaries of understanding for the students that this is about the skills required of the environment, not about the situation in Panama.”

Though public sentiment between the countries has ebbed and flowed in the decades that followed Panama’s 1994 formal abolishment of its standing army — several years after a U.S. military invasion ousted military dictator Manuel Noriega — those tensions were absent from interactions Military Times observed among the service members during the course.

Eagen said the U.S. is mindful of the pride Panamanians take in their nation’s sovereignty. The Army, he added, has been purposeful in approaching the course’s renewed partnership with an emphasis on learning from — rather than simply teaching — its Panamanian counterparts.
Eve Sampson is a reporter and former Army officer. She has covered conflict across the world, writing for The New York Times, The Washington Post and The Associated Press.
